subtopic: INVESTIGATION OF SUBSIDIARY OF TELEPHONE OR TELEGRAPH COMPANIES

speechtext: Mr. G. R. GEARY (South Toronto) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 63, to amend the Railway Act, (Investigation of subsidiary of telephone or telegraph companies).

subtopic: INVESTIGATION OF SUBSIDIARY OF TELEPHONE OR TELEGRAPH COMPANIES
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: INVESTIGATION OF SUBSIDIARY OF TELEPHONE OR TELEGRAPH COMPANIES
speechtext:
When an application comes before the Board of Railway Commissioners to fix the rates of a telephone or telegraph com-

pany, either by way of reduction or increase of such rates, the- financial condition of the company is a matter of which the board must make itself fully aware, because on the financial condition of the company, its assets and its liabilities, its income and expenditure, is based as a rule the decision of the board as to whether the rates should be increased or reduced. It is suggested that a company such as this may conceal a certain important part of its affairs by the formation of a subsidiary company or the acquiring of another company to which that portion of its affairs may be transferred for treatment.
Under the act there is no jurisdiction in the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada to investigate the affairs of such a company, that is of a subsidiary or acquired company such as I have described. It is beyond my comprehension why an investigation into the affairs of a company Should stop at the point where that company has transferred a part of its affairs to another company which is a subsidiary or controlled company but which in reality is a part of itself. The purpose of this bill is to remove what I submit to the house is an absurdity by giving jurisdiction to the Board of Railway Commissioners to inquire into the affairs of such a subsidiary or controlled company.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: THE BUDGET DEBATE-FORTY MINUTE RULE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: THE BUDGET DEBATE-FORTY MINUTE RULE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak on what I think is properly a question of privilege. The privileges of the

The Budget-Forty Minute Rule
house are involved, and also the special privileges that some hon. members seek to obtain. Last session we revised the rules limiting speeches to forty minutes and setting eleven o'clock as the hour of adjournment. This was done to shorten debate and expedite the business of the house-a result that we who come from a long distance and have to spend months here are very desirous to obtain. But I doubt very much whether this result will be obtained unless we curb certain practices that seem to me to have grown up during the last few weeks.
While there may be some advantages in the new rules, there are also some disadvantages. It seems to me that the new rules have encouraged the practice-I do not use the term offensively but simply for want of something more apt-of jockeying for position. W'e all understand why hon. members should wish to get first place on the orders of the day. It is more pleasant to speak to a full house and full galleries than to empty benches. Naturally also the member, if he has a weakness for newspaper publicity, has an opportunity to have his vanity gratified. This, I suppose, is inevitable. The reporters are probably limited to so much space, and their copy, I expect, is prepared early in the evening.
We have now been debating the budget for three weeks. In the early days of the debate it might have been allowable to adjourn early because of lack of preparation on the part of hon. members. But at this late stage there is no reason why any member should not be prepared to speak at the time assigned him by the whips. Last Monday I began to speak at ten o'clock. On Tuesday the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) began to speak at ten o'clock. One day last week the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) began his speech so late in the evening that he had to complete it next day. But last night, as on some former occasions, the debate was adjourned at ten o'clock. The hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who was leading the house, said he had no objections if it did not interfere with the arrangement to conclude the debate next Tuesday. But the government is not the only one affected; the privileges of hon. members are interfered with. Possibly the early adjournment last night may debar some hon. member from taking part in the debate.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that there would be some difficulty in having a hard and fast rule that you could apply with the same impartiality as the forty-minute rule; but I would suggest to the house the impropriety 56103-73
of any member at this late stage of the debate asking for an adjournment at ten o'clock. Could there not be a gentleman's agreement under which any member would be willing to take a sporting chance of what comes to him in the matter of time? I know it has been the custom to allow the adjournment to go to the different parties and groups in rotation, but that custom could still be observed without needlessly prolonging the time of debate or interfering with the privileges of any hon. member.

subtopic: THE BUDGET DEBATE-FORTY MINUTE RULE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw the attention of the house to a very difficult situation that affects many of our members under the forty-minute rule. The other evening when I was speaking I sat down at the end of thirty minutes, believing that I had exhausted the time allotted to me. Of course, I had to depend upon my colleagues to let me know when my forty minutes had expired. Now, in order to facilitate the business of the house and enable hon. members to know how their time is passing, I would suggest that on the table there should be an electric button within easy reach of the Clerk by which he could indicate the passage of the forty minutes by switching on near the clocks a green light and a red light at fifteen and thirty-minute periods respectively. Then an hon. member would know when to begin his peroration. An electrician could set up such a device in a short time. It is very difficult for hon. members to keep an accurate check on the hon. gentleman who may have the floor. For instance, yesterday I timed the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) and other hon. members, and found my timing did not agree with that kept by other members.

subtopic: THE BUDGET DEBATE-FORTY MINUTE RULE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, might I say that this shows the utter absurdity of the rule.

subtopic: THE BUDGET DEBATE-FORTY MINUTE RULE
speechtext:
Of course, this is a matter for the house to decide. Personally I would not object to the green and red lights -I know the meaning of the two colours. But I should like the arrangement to be automatic so that I might depend on the clock and not on my own judgment, well remembering the words of Pope:
'Tis with our judgments as our watches, none
Go just alike, yet each believes his own.
I should like every hon. member to rely on the clocks when I have to say time!" Of course, it is understood that the clocks are under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott).

The Budget-Mr. Robinson

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, March 8, consideration of the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb (Minister of Finance), that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Cahan and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Fansher (East Lambton).

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset allow me to assure you that I shall not consume my full forty minutes. This debate has now been in progress for three weeks, and there is very little left for private members to say at this late stage. Therefore I shall confine myself in what I have to say to the important constituency of West Essex, which comprises the city of Windsor, the towns of Sandwich and 0 jib way, and the townships of Sandwich East and Sandwich WTest; a constituency which is attracting the attention of the whole Dominion at the present time owing to the extensive developments now going on there.
But before I deal with my subject I should like to make a couple of references to the speech delivered last evening by the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard). I want to remind him that charity

begins at home; and when he suggests that there should be a further cut in the price of automobiles of from 15 to 20 per cent, a reduction such as the industry could not possibly stand, it seems to me that it would be more apropos if the hon. gentleman would advise that the industries he controls in Sherbrooke, which have a protection of from 30 to 35 per cent, should suffer a similar reduction.
The hon. gentleman said that no suggestion had come from the opposition as to giving employment to the unemployed. Apparently he has not followed the debate, but as I proceed I will suggest to him where all the unemployed in Canada might be taken care of if certain policies were carried out. This unemployment problem is in my opinion the most serious we have to deal with in this country, if for no other reason than the importance of keeping our Canadians at home. A situation has prevailed in Windsor during the past two years which is new to us in the way of unemployment. There are several reasons for this. I am informed that when people from the British Isles are on the steamships crossing the Atlantic and do not know exactly where they are going to settle when they come to this country, officers, or passengers as the case may be, advise them, '''Oh, go to the border cities; you will get a job there at from $4 to S5 a day". Unfortunately this has not been the case since the reduction in the automobile tariff. Further, we have another situation there for the relief of which I think we should have some assistance from the government. I refer to deportations from the United States of Canadian citizens most of whom are of foreign birth, and who entered that country illegally: when they are deported back to Canada they are dumped into Windsor and in most cases become a charge on the city. The result is that the charity funds of the municipal council of Windsor are growing by leaps and bounds to take care of these unemployed.
According to the chamber of commerce returns regarding employment in the border cities, in September, 1926, 74 firms out of 114 gave a return of 11,337 men employed. In September, 1927, the number was 8,661, showing a decrease of 2,676. I want to be fair about this, and I will say that conditions are better chiefly on account of the Ford Motor Company having started. In November, 1926, the employment figure was 11,349 and in November, 1927, 10,304, still a decrease of
I, 045. In December, 1926, the figure was
II,	034 and in December, 1927, 10,171, or r decrease of 863.

The Budget-Mr. Robinson
Referring to the question of unemployment, I wish to read certain remarks made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) in Winnipeg. I quote the following from the Montreal Gazette:
Unemployment Problem
Heenan Gets Suggestions from Manitoba Officials
Winnipeg, February 25.-The problem of unemployment is the most gigantic task the Canadian government has to face, and the co-operation of municipal, provincial and private bodies would be necessary before it could be solved, stated Hon. Peter Heenan, federal Minister of Labor at a meeting to-day attended by members of the legislature, provincial officials, aldermen of the city and board of trade members.
Mr. Heenan promised to take the various suggestions back to Ottawa and place them before the departments involved.
I could suggest many other ways of finding . employment for thousands more in the border cities, but we are faced with so many difficulties in connection with the continual tinkering with the tariff, and reductions which are made from year to year, that industry does not know where it stands. Let me give to the house a concrete illustration. In the border cities we have a drop forging plant whose expenditure on plant and machinery is some $1,500,000, and they are in competition with similar plants in the United States. Let us suppose that General Motors in the United States have from seventy to eighty different plants; they take their overhead in connection with all these plants at, say, 25 per cent, dividing it proportionately among them. The overhead in drop forging plants is higher than in any other line of industry owing to the high cost of drop forging machinery, dies, tools, et cetera. The proportion should be 75 per cent. This concern to which I have reference put in their tender for an export business in Canada on which they would get a drawback of 99 per cent. I might mention, by the way, that the drop forging plants in Canada have to import their machinery, steel, dies, tools, oil, coal, et cetera. The Canadian concern underbid the American competitors by 7i per cent and the Americans immediately determined to meet the price and so they got the order. To my mind there should be something in the customs regulations whereby Canadian industry might be protected against such unfair competition. I submit that an expert should go into the drop forging plants in the United States to ascertain their cost of manufacturing, comparing it with the cost in the Canadian plants, taking the respective invoices. I am sure that in most cases the
Canadian plant could not manufacture at the same price.
A good deal has been said about emigration from Canada. I want to give the figures from the American consular office at Windsor for the years 1926 and 1927. I have them here month by month but I will not burden the house with them. For the first six months in 1926 vises were issued to 2,357 Canadian born citizens who desired to reside permanently in the United States. In the first six months of 1927 the number was 2,090, a difference of 267. The figures for the last six months of 1927 show an entirely different state of things. For the last six months of 1926, 2,189 Canadian citizens took out vises to live in the United States whereas in the last six months of 1927 there were 4,070 or 1,881 more than in the corresponding six months of 1926.
My remedy for unemployment-and this is my answer to the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard)-is that if the government would cease tinkering with the tariff on agricultural machinery and automobiles, and let us manufacture our raw materials into the finished product they could find employment for 100,000 more in this country. We are continually increasing our importations of manufactured goods which should be produced in this country, and to offset that the government policy is to increase our foreign trade. We all know that the best market for the farmer and the Canadian manufacturer is our home market; we should look after that market first and develop the foreign market afterwards.
There is one other thing to which I would like to direct the attention of the Minister of Finance; I refer to old age pensions. If the government would increase the allowance under the old age pension scheme I am sure it would help the municipalities throughout the country which are at present maintaining houses of refuge and similar institutions. It would also be of great assistance to the Salvation Army and other charitable organizations, because a good many of these old people would come under the old age pension scheme and the 'municipalities would not have to shoulder the whole burden.
There is another suggestion I have to offer, which would benefit the border cities throughout Canada, and perhaps particularly those in Ontario. Since we have obtained a sane liquor law in Ontario many Americans who desire to enjoy greater	freedom, and
especially those who are British bom, would like to live on the Canadian side of the border, and of course we would like to have them here.	My suggestion is that if an.
The Budget-Mr. Robinson

American citizen wishes to live in Canada, a man whose business is entirely in the United States and whose entire revenue is derived in that country, he should be allowed to bring his automobile into this country in bond. Many people who would like to come to Canada seem to find that the great stumbling block; they have to pay duty on their automobiles while their household goods are brought in free, and in many cases their automobiles are used chiefly in their business. This arrangement would be reciprocal, to a certain extent.
A great deal has been said about the automobile industry, and in that conection I would like to draw to the attention of the Minister of Finance the fact that in 1927 our importations of automobiles and parts were valued at $65,497,721. In 1926 these importations were valued at $54,305,111, which shows an increase of 111,192,611 in one year. On the floor of this house two years ago the minister stated that his policy would force automobile manufacturers doing business in Canada to establish plants here, but that has not been the case. The largest single items in the importation of automobiles were Hudson and Essex cars, the production of which does not involve one day of Canadian labour. Also in this connection it is worthy of note that the change in the tariff on automobiles has practically eliminated the Canadian manufacturer of trucks and busses from the markets of the Canadian west. The Gotfredson corporation, which up to that time doubled its business every year, now finds it very difficult to carry on. Some associates of mine, together with myself, put $35,000 into the stock of that company, which sold at $25 a share; today you cannot sell the stock. It is listed on the Toronto Stock Exchange at $8 bid and $9 asked, and there are no transactions taking place in it. I am told that in the maritime provinces and in British Columbia the United States manufacturers of trucks and buses will drive their cars a thousand or two thousand miles over muddy roads to the border; then m some cases will have a truck tow them to some customs house, and have a valuator value them as second-hand trucks or buses. In this way they will only pay duty on about one-third of the value of the car, so the Canadian manufacturers cannot compete against them. I believe that defect has been remedied to some extent, but as yet the business has not come back to the Canadian manufacturers.
Another very important item is the farm tractor, which was put on the free list as a war measure to increase production on the

farms. In 1924 we imported 5,236 tractors with a total value of $3,651,502; in 1925 we imported 2,200 having a total value of $1,410,554, while in 1926 we imported 6,895 tractors, valued at $5,153,120. I have secured the figures for 1927 from the Bureau of Statistics; in that year 15,651 tractors worth $1,400 each were imported, the total value being $12,091,910. In addition to that 231 farm tractor engines were imported in 1927, and these were valued at $491,728. Surely, even if nothing else can be done, this material should be allowed into Canada free to be machined and assembled in this country, which would provide employment for a large number of workers. The Ford Motor Company, at Walkerville bought a fifty acre plot of land for the construction of a building and equipment to manufacture Ford tractors, but since tractors have been placed on the free list thi3 company cannot compete with the parent concern in Detroit, so the matter was allowed to drop. I have no doubt, however, that if a duty were placed on tractors, as certainly should be done, the Ford company would proceed to manufacture tractors in Canada and perhaps other companies would start up in addition.
Now I would like to say just a word with regard to the tobacco industry. We held meetings in Chatham and Windsor as well as throughout the entire southwestern part of Ontario at which we had the honour of the presence of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) and his deputy. These gentlemen visited that district twice, and we came to parliament expecting some result. What has happened? They have not said a word with refrence to the position of that industry to-day. Apparently the government will not take advice or suggestions coming from this side of the house, ibut I think it is the duty of those members representing that part of Ontario to say something on behalf of that industry. Everyone expected a reasonable reduction of the excise duty on cigarettes, which would reduce the smuggling of these articles and would greatly help the tobacco industry, but they were disappointed. Thera is no doubt that this should be done and also that the excise tax on cigars should be reduced. We should also raise our duty against raw leaf tobacco to the level of the United States tariff against us. It seems a shame when we consider that w7e import some 17,000,000 pounds of tobacco from the United States which could be very well supplied by our own farmers.
Now I would like to read a couple of extracts to show what the people of the United States think of a high protective tariff, and

The Budget-Mr. Robinson
what they consider it has done for the manufacturer and farmer of that country. President Coolidge speaking before the Union League of Philadelphia on November 17, 1927, regarding the benefits derived from the tariff by all classes in the United States, made the following statements:
Without the influence of a protective tariff, it would never have been possible for our country to reach its present stage of diversified development with its liberal rate of wages, its unprecedented distribution of wealth, and its high standards of living. If these conditions are to be maintained, that policy will have to be continued. In some few lines we can compete with all the world, but in general our agriculture and our industry, are compelled to make a larger outlay to provide their establishment, pay a very much higher rate of wages, and therefore find their costs of production are greater than in foreign countries.
Any material reduction in our general tariff rates would ultimately result in a drastic deflation of agricultural and industrial values, in the rate of wages, and in the standards of living. Under our present system our foreign commerce has reached the highest peace-time record and our national income has steadily increased to the enormous proportion of $90,000,000,000, for the last calendar year. This represents a volume of production and trade far in excess of that which any other country ever reached. It is the zenith of our prosperity. All of this should be considered in any appraisal of the worth of our long-established policy.
While we have placed the enterprise of the country unreservedly in private hands, we have adopted a system of government regulation and denounced by law- restraints of trade and unfair practices in trade, in order that the public might have the full benefits of all fair competition and the opportunities of our commerce be equally free to all. Privilege has no place in either our political or economic system.
I quote further from the newspaper called the South Dakota Chief, published in Iroquois, which is a farming community, to the following effect:
What Protection Has done
Here is a voice from the west (The Voice of the Iroquois, S.D., Chief) raised in championship of the present tariff law:
. As a matter of fact, things have turned out just as the protectionists predicted. Wages have gone up because the workers have been protected from cheap European competition. And the great assured home market has permitted the manufacturers so to increase their production and reduce manufacturing costs that the cost of living has not increased. We have therefore at this time what would seem to the theoretical economist an impossible condition- an increase in wages and a reduction in the cost of living. The theorist told us that it couldn't be done, but the theorists as a rule are free traders, internationalists and whatnot. They fail to give due weight to the American idea of standardized production.
Before closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to give a few facts regarding the Canadian Steel Corporation in Ojibway in my riding, as it has
been mentioned two or three times in this house. I can assure you that I know whereof I speak because I had the honcfur to succeed the late Hon. W. C. Kennedy in the council of Ojibway. When the United States Steel Corporation located at Ojibway, in Essex county, and formed the Canadian Steel Corporation, it was their intention to manufacture chiefly iron and steel products, which at that time were not being produced in Canada. After expending some nine or ten million dollars, work was stopped in 1922 owing to the fact that the present government were pledged to carry out their platform of 1919, and the subsequent tinkering with the tariff in the iron and steel industry confirmed their judgment of 1922. The corporation is at the present time removing its wire mill from Hamilton to Ojibway, the only development which has taken place in recent years, to the detriment of the former city. This factory will employ from one hundred to two hundred men when working at full capacity. I can say, without fear of contradiction, that if the tariff on iron and steel is stabilized and the industry receives the protection to which it is entitled against unfair competition the Canadian Steel Corporation is only too anxious to go ahead with its project which will involve the expenditure of millions of dollars and the employment of many thousand men. My opponent in the last election stated that if the Liberals were returned to power they would force the Canadian Steel Corporation to go ahead and produce. And to use his own words they would have to "play ball or get off the diamond." This attitude influenced a large number of votes in the locality of the steel corporation. I should like to ask the government whether it is its intention to carry out that promise and if so when? I will give the government credit for carrying out the Liberal candidate's promise in the by-election of 1923 in North Essex. Mr. Healey promised at that time that if he was elected the government would construct a breakwater at Belle River. After his election the government promptly carried out the work at a cost to the people of Canada of $30,000.
There has been a good deal of publicity lately in connection with the subject of a new post office at Windsor, and I sincerely hope the government intends to go on with that work. The present post office was erected, I think, in 1879 or 1880 when Windsor was a town of 5,000 population. Now it is a city of over 65,000 and yet our postal facilities are the same as they were forty-seven years ago. Those facilities are really
The Budget-Mr. Robinson

a disgrace when you consider the importance of Windsor and its proximity to a large city like Detroit. There are thousands of people who come over from Detroit and send mail from the Windsor post office. Sometimes the people are crowded there like sardines in a box. The office does not possess even the necessary facilities for the writing of postcards. If I can do anything to bring about an improvement in the conditions I shall be most happy to do so. I am in accord with my colleague and friend from East Essex (Mr. Odette) who stated, I believe the present site can be sold for a price that will pay for the construction of a new post office.
There is just one more subject I wish to refer to and then I shall be through. That is the removal of the duty on coal in the interests of the salt industry. We all know that most of the salt used in Canada comes from Essex county, from the Canadian Salt Company's works, but I do not think that company ever begged the government to take the duty off coal. What they wanted was a duty to keep foreign salt out of Canada and to preserve the salt market for Canadian manufacturers.
Mr. E. C. ST-PERE (Hochelaga) (Translation) :	Mr. Speaker, I read somewhere that
the Right Hon. Lloyd George, in the course of a lecture given in an English university, advised those who destined themselves to politics, to first begin by being good listeners. Since the outset of this debate on the budget, I endeavoured to listen well, I tried to note all the arguments which were put forth, both for and against the budget proposals. As it would take me too much time to discuss them fully and do them justice, I shall content myself with the time allotted by the new rules of the house, to review as briefly as possible the contentions of the various speakers who followed one another during the course of this debate.
I shall abstain myself from adding further compliments to the torrent of congratulations with which the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has been overwhelmed.
I shall only say that he simply did his duty towards our country, and that is for him the greatest satisfaction.
As every business man does, it is well to consider what have been our revenues and our expenditures during the course of the last fiscal year. I must say, together with all those who have impartially considered the state of our finances up to date, that the sound administration of the Minister of Finance has given us what all business men

first expect: a surplus of revenues over expenditures. Our finances are therefore in a very sound condition.
With regard to the budget proposals, the general approval of the country amply proves that it has given satisfaction to everybody. No doubt there will be found-and that is so to speak the continual enforcing of the old proverb which says the fortunes of one make the misfortunes of another-there will be found critics who, notwithstanding the general approval, will always find fault simply for political purposes.
The wiping out of the sales tax, whatever may be said against it, has given satisfaction to the business people of this country; and as recently as last week, a great financier of Montreal told me that the gradual reduction carried out by the hon. Minister of Finance, would certainly prevent a great number of dealers suffering very appreciable losses in the sale of their goods.
The income tax was a measure imposed owing to uncontrollable events, and a great number who are at present victims are not responsible for it. I do not wish to go back and discuss war events, I never have recourse to such arguments in the course of my political campaigns, yet during the great war, I have seen in my riding some of those large manufacturers, of those so called patriots of that period, who now so loudly call for the entire wiping out of the income tax, trying to shelter themselves by paying their employees, from the president down to the humblest secretary, large bonuses, and thus avoid paying the government the necessary amounts for the upkeep of the country.
The hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) was telling us yesterday that the owners of large fortunes should especially be called upon to pay. I fully agree with him I even would go one step further. May I ask the hon. Minister of Finance to take good note of the remark I am now making. Young people, in my native province, are advised1 to practise economy, parsimony is recommended to them so as to shelter them when rainy days come. Now, I state that the limit of exemption from taxation under the income tax, should be higher than $4,000. And this is why: in our province and especially in the workmen's quarters of Montreal-I say it to their praise-the small property is held by workmen, it belongs to people who have saved, who have denied themselves all the luxuries that simple life can afford to the humblest citizen of this country, and from this taxable $4,000, the person taxed on said amount must economize for the future. He must pay from

The Budget-Mr. St. Pere
that amount the insurance policy in prevision of rainy days, which amount he deducts so as to provide for his family in case of misfortunes. He must foresee many things. He must especially set aside savings to meet the taxes for local improvements in cities. Perhaps, you will say that these taxes for local improvements which you state he must pay each year, are deducted from his annual budget. I deny this, because in the city of Montreal, as elsewhere, local improvement taxes are payable sometimes only three or four years after the work i3 completed. Take the amount of $160 per year which small property owners are called upon to pay, calculate that amount for ten years ahead with compound interests, and I ask you if truly the Dominion government by taxing that little income does not by this fact give a premium to carelessness and work to unroot among us the spirit of economy which is a trait of the French Canadian people.
I now come to the remittance of the income tax to large corporations. I have never been, sir, an extremist. I consider that the large corporations should not be treated as outcasts, but to infer from this that we must, at each claim they put forth, bow our heads for political purposes and grant their claims, I say no. Quite recently, a delegation composed of the municipal authorities of Montreal and a great number of representatives of our public corporations came up to Ottawa to interview the hon. Minister of Finance. I must state that, at first, I appeared to approve the request of the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company, but as soon as I learned the details of their operations, I changed entirely my opinion. It matters little whether it is the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company or any other corporation which come to us to obtain a reduction in taxes, I clearly state and without restriction that I am opposed to such reduction. And why this great company known as the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company, that large corporation distributor ol power, which producing but little power- buying it as it does from various corporations and then selling it at a profit to the consumers of the city of Montreal-why this company, I say, should not pay taxes like the others. I am at a loss to say. This large industry does not limit its operation simply to the distribution of electricity, but it sells moreover a great number of house commodities, etc. It sells coal-and I shall deal squarely with it on this matter-I admit that the coke which it sells obliges in some way our population by allowing it to purchase fuel at lower prices than American anthracite. But basing ourselves on such a principle, why should we not exempt
from the income tax the small merchants of Montreal who sell electric stoves, toasters, beside all the coal dealers who supply the population with the fuel needed for heating purposes?
Mr. Speaker, the hon. Minister of Finance deserves our congratulations for having taught that delegation, which came up here sometime ago, a lesson that, no doubt, made it understand that the Minister of Finance for Canada was well posted on the operations of this company, and on no account would he change his opinion that those who should pay taxes to the country-there is an economic principle involved-are those who are most capable of doing so.
One word on the tariff question. I am no more an extremist as regards the tariff than I am on other matters. I do not consider the tariff as a doctrine, but as a policy which adapts itself to circumstances. And since I am free to state it from my seat in the House of Commons, there is an industry in my riding-one making cotton goods-an industry which notwithstanding the tariff reduction of 71% will not lose any of its profits. It is an industry very highly protected. I am speaking of the Dominion Textile Co. This year, that company made very large profits, and as from time to time it makes changes in its mills, I trust that it will not take advantage of such a circumstance to tell its employees-and, sir, its employees are for the most part people of my race-'"This lowering of the tariff will bring about a decrease in your wages". When these workers threaten to strike, the company sends to the counties of the lower St. Lawrence, a new kind of recruiters who use to entice to the county of Hochelaga poorly paid workmen. It is often said that corporations have no soul. I admit it, but I ask of those who profit-I shall not say of government money-but I ask of those who profit from a protective tariff, which is a guarantee against the invasion of American cotton goods, and I shall even say against the English cotton goods, to show that they are human and pay their employees wages, which will allow them to exist and not wages which, on an average-these are statistics taken from the department of Labour- amount for each of these workers to the pitiful sum of six hundred and a few dollars per year. Our opponents, whom I take the treedom of always calling friends, like to state a little everywhere that protection, which should be adopted, would stem the tide of emigration towards the United States. I would advise them to consult the leaders of the labour unions, and ask them if they
The Budget-Mr. St. Pere

agree with the assertions which the Conservatives advocate at present and which they always advocate, assertions which made the subject of their electoral campaign.
Strictly speaking, I represent the largest riding of workmen in Canada, and I am still wondering if some day I would receive a protest of that kind from my electors. I state that protection never safeguarded the interests of the workmen. No, protection never protected the workman. If the workman, today, receives protection, he owes it to the excellent organisation of the workers' unions, he owes it to his spirit of work, to his initiative, to the constant improvement in the machinery which he uses in his work and which facilitates mass production.
Our opponents further tell us that the United States are an Eden for those who emigrate there. I shall not quote to them a page of ancient history; I shall not even tell them that their arguments are refuted by statistics of a year old; let me, sir, quote from an article published on March 4 last, in the Sunday edition of the World of New York, and signed by Charles Stelzle, organiser and past superintendent of the Temple of work of New York. I shall give the English text, so that our opponents will not charge me with misrepresenting the facts and still less the text. I kindly ask my hon. colleagues of the English language to listen to it. The text reads as follows:
Based upon reports received from the Welfare Council of New York City, the President of the State Federation of Labour, the President of the Central Trades and Labour Council of New York City, the Commissioner of the Department of Licenses of New York City, the Superintendent of the Municipal Lodging House, and various welfare agencies, as well as from figures produced by the Department of Labour itself, it was demonstrated that there is "an extensive amount of unemployment, and serious distress has been caused on this account."
That there is a considerable amount of unemployment in New York City is reported by practically every agency of a social, industrial and philanthropic character. An increase in the number and the length of breadlines, the crowding of the Municipal Lodging House, the growing number of respectable-looking beggars on the streets, the great excess of situations wanted over help wanted advertisements in the daily newspapers, particularly as compared with those of recent years, the filling up of the poorer class of lodging houses, the increase in the amount of relief given by social agencies to families suffering because of the unemployment of bread-winners, the unusual amount of credit being asked for in neighborhood stores are a few of the signs which point to an increase in unemployment.
Serious Distress Caused by Situation
We are told by the Urban League, which looks after the Negro population of the city, that while in January, 1927, it had 365
TMr. St. Pere.]
applicants for every 100 jobs, in January, 1928, there were 1,175 applicants for every 100 jobs. The Y.M.C.A. and the Vocational Service for Juniors report much the same kind of a situation. Commercial employment agencies placing office and clerical help report a 100 per cent increase in the number of applicants for jobs; and the agencies for hotel and restaurant workers say that there is a stream of applicants, with no jobs available. This lack of employment is found not only among the unskilled, but in many of the skilled trades. The Amalgamated Clothing Workers, with a membership of 45,000, reports
15,000	out of work.
As is the case during every winter, large numbers of men have come to New York from rural districts and labour camps with the expectation of finding jobs. A considerable number have come from the coal fields of Pennsylvania and Ohio because of the strikes in these regions, and from New England towns where the textile industry has for so long a time been demoralized.
No One Prepares For the Cycles
In spite of the fact that unemployment comes regularly in cycles-from seven to ten years apart-scarcely anybody seems ever to get ready for its recurrence. We have conferences of the same "experts", but by the time that their program has been formulated the necessity for putting it into operation has gone by. Even the cause of unemployment seems to remain a mystery. At any rate there is a greatly diversified opinion as to what is responsible for it. Some authorities believe that it is a purely psychological situation; the Socialists charge it up to the competitive system; the politicians out of office attribute it to the Administration that is in power; at various times Wall Street has been held responsible; for a good many years it was charged up to our excess immigrant population.
Mr. Speaker, here and there, we hear that we must see that a great flood of immigrants flow's into the country so as to bring back prosperity among us. I do not believe in intensive immigration. Such immigration lends itself greatly to unemployment, and as I am first a Canadian, I would ask that the immigrants-it is of little import where they come from, whether it is from England or elsewhere

who come to us disguised as farmhands and who for the most part conceal able mechanics, must not come here-and this I have the proof every day in my riding-ready to replace at a moments notice our able mechanics, Irish, French Canadians and English, who are in this country.

speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation):	We have
established everywhere in our various provinces technical schools; we encourage young people to follow the courses given there, and on the first occasion-I may say that sometimes partiality and unfairness has something to do with it-one of our electors or a friend that we consider and his employer considers as an able mechanic, finds himself replaced

The Budget-Mr. St. Pere
without notice by a mechanic who hails from Leeds or elsewhere. Canada for Canadians, always! That is why I am opposed to an intensive immigration; the cries of those who tell us here and there that Canada must be peopled by English-speaking subjects, is of little import; Canada is sufficiently vast to welcome individuals of every language and nationality. Canada will increase its population, the west will increase its population when the synods from Kingston, etc., will cease their cries that people fear French Canadian immigration in the west, when certain Canadians ill-advised, who are far from advocating national unity, will cease to try and root out, as they would do a plague, the French Canadian element from the population of certain provinces.
Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to an intensive immigration. It is quite right that we should bring in farm-help. On that score, I congratulate the Canadian National Railways for its spirit of initiative in bringing, for the farmers of Quebec, farm help speaking the language of the majority of people in that province. I also wish to congratulate certain other organizations for their efforts to increase the population of our country by bringing in desirable settlers.
The hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Bell) whom I might designate a sower of fear-they shot those people during the war -was saying the other day that he often met on the streets of Montreal people who asked for charity. I grew up in Montreal, I know my city better than the member for St. Antoine and I want to tell him, unfortunately for the argument which he seems to bring in support of his contention, that the only people we meet and who beg a ten cent piece for a nights' shelter or five cents for food-rihat is called a plate of beans- are immigrants; because those among us who are in want have no need to have recourse to begging; our splendid philanthropic societies amply suffice for their needs.
One further word on emigration. Why so much bewail over the emigration of our people. The French Canadian loves, from time to time, to change his abode. If our people had not emigrated from Quebec to other provinces, and especially to the western provinces, I am wondering if the people of the west would have large cities like they have to-day. If there had not been a Lacombe to help the Canadian Pacific in laying its steel ribbon across the western provinces, I wonder what they would have done. A kind member,-a harmless chap hailing from British Columbia-told us-and I wish to refute this error-that he also deplored the emigration of the people from
Quebec to the United States. Well! that province of Quebec how one likes it eadh time it is required to point to it to prop up a poor argument. It is said:	The people of the province of Quebec emigrate to the United States, and once there, forget their religion. Another political falsehood, another trick of politics. It is of little import that they emigrate to the United States or elsewhere, the first thought of a French Canadian is to have a home near his church, and the institutions of the French Canadians in New England and everywhere amply prove that they do neither lose their faith nor language, notwithstanding their emigration to foreign lands.
Before resuming my seat, allow me, sir, to make a few remarks with regard to our farmers. At election time, one comes to them, one endeavours to tell them that their conditions are pitiable. But under whose rule have our farmers emigrated to the United States, if it is not under that of the Conservatives? Let me put the question to the Conservatives of to-day: what have your predecessors done to stem this emigration? Nothing. Whatever was done for the farmers, to improve their lot, was done under the Liberal governments. Recently, our farmers came up to Ottawa, as a delegation, to ask the Minister of Finance, when he brings down his supplementary estimates to kindly include an item so as to meet the request presented by the association of breeders of the province of Quebec. The province of Quebec and the French Canadian members of this house are not here to beg for sympathy. We listened attentively and we generously made grants to the people of the Maritime provinces when they put forth their claims. And I tell the people of the west again that we did the same thing for them. Quebec only claims its due. Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to say so, in many parts of my province, prosperous villages are entirely deprived of railway communication; Gaspe, Bonaventure, Yamaska, and I shall even add Joliette, my native place-need railways to help in their development. I would ask the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), to kindly accede to our just claims. During many years people from Quebec were asked to go and settle the New Ontario and the Canadian west. There aTe certain districts in the west where our people settled and-I am proud to say-they are considered as farmers very much attached to their lands and hard workers. These farmers are deprived, after years of hard labour, of communication which would help them to give their families appreciable ease. I trust that the Minister of Railways will listen and grant them their just claims.
The Budget-Mr. St. Pere

Mr. Speaker, there is another question-and I broach it with all the necessary reserve-it is the St. Lawrence waterway scheme. The government has not come to a decision in regard to this matter. Opinions in Montreal are divided on this question, and as the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard), stated last night, if by chance we decided to build that St. Lawrence waterway, I would ask- for that part extending along the shores of Quebec and which would supply power to many of our industries and electric light to our population-that the rights of developing these powers rest with the government, it is of little import whether it be federal or provincial. The consumers of Ottawa pay a minimum rate for lighting purposes while those of Montreal are being imposed upon.
I want to point out to this house that the statements made recently by a senator in no way pledges the members from Montreal. Let us not so quickly be led to believe that this St. Lawrence waterway scheme will join the waters of the Pactole to those of the St. Lawrence. Let us await events before coming to a definite conclusion on the subject. I shall close my remarks. From what I have heard up to now, Mr. Speaker, the party which sits to your left is a party of negation. It denies the general satisfaction of the people of Canada; that party denies the prosperity of our country; lastly it denies the worth of all competent persons who have given the government a certificate of honesty and good administration. It is the party of negation. I gladly rally to the party which is open to evidence, which is aware that Canad'a is not a perfect nation, but that all is susceptible of being perfected; I rally to that party which believes in not letting the light under the bushel but rather wants to have it enlighten the more, those to whom the people confided, since 1921, the care of guiding the national destinies of this country.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel impelled to take up the time of the house this afternoon because so little of a constructive nature has been brought forward by the hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Forke) either this year or last dealing with the very serious question of population, that I fear the country at large and even some of the hon. members might reasonably conclude that this, the greatest issue before parliament, cannot be successfully solved.
My good friend, the Minister of Immigration, in the committee on agriculture yesterday expressed his great disappointment that we on this side of the house had not put

forward definite proposals for him to consider. His sincere expression indicates to me his despair,-after two years, of getting any real suggestions from his own associates. His appeal has not fallen on deaf ears.
In response to his request, I propose this afternoon to disregard all political strategy and run the risk of criticism in submitting for the consideration of the hon. minister and this house a program which I believe will restore our immigration to the favourable figures we enjoyed in the years immediately preceding the war.
The limited time at my disposal-forty minutes-permits me to submit only a general or skeleton outline of the development which I think the government should undertake I will be prepared, however, as opportunity offers to support the practicability of my proposals.
Hon members treat our population problem as a dual one-immigration and emigration. As a matter of fact, we have only one problem. Give us satisfactory immigration and we will have no emigration to worry about. In 1913, when 400.000 immigrants entered Canada, 139 000 of them came from the United States. That year only 14 165 of our people went to that country. We gained
125.000	on them in 1913. We will do it again when we get a real immigration movement under way.
In order that they may enjoy a higher status in life, over 185,000 Canadian boys and girls attended high school last year;
65.000	students were registered in our universities and colleges. Our universities are not turning out farmers. Higher 'education is taking our boys and girls off the farms. If they cannot find useful employment in the business structure of their own country they can always go to the United States. There- thanks to the sterling qualities they inherit from their forefathers-they receive a preference over others and are welcomed as new citizens in every city from New York to San Francisco.
I will confine my remarks to-day to the development of our unoccupied lands-our greatest natural resource. A steadily increasing agricultural population will demand and support a growing national business structure. More people on farms necessitates a corresponding increase in our cities and towns resulting in a demand for more business and professional men and women-more employment for labour of all kinds. Only in this way can our young people find the opportunities they must have if they are to remain in Canada.

The Budget-Mr. McRae
Let us be practical in these matters. We must have some one to do the basic work of the country if the boy or girl of this or future generations who graduates from our educational institutions is to find congenial employment at home.
I entirely agree with the policy of confining our immigration efforts to prospective farmers and domestic servants. It is my humble opinion that we should not encourage the immigration of men or women only qualified for city life. The drift to the cities, which is one of the things we will have to contend with, will supply our city population for many years to come. In common with the United States our problem of the future will be to keep our people on the farms
Our immigration records clearly show that we must provide employment for our incoming immigrants to assist them to get on their feet. From 1881 to 1885, when we were getting very satisfactory immigration for those days, the Canadian Pacific was under construction. Hon. members will recall that when we enjoyed our greatest prolonged period of successful immigration, from 1903 to 1913, we were carrying on a tremendous program of railway construction in this country. The National Transcontinental and the then Canadian Northern were built from coast to coast.
There is no big construction program before the country at this time. Something must be attempted if we are to take care of a large immigration. The question is what development program can we undertake which will be safe, sound, and ultimately pay the interest on the capital invested-which will not add unduly to the present burden of taxation and will at the same time afford the necessary grub-stake for our incoming settlers.
I suggest that the only program available is the development of the land on which we propose to put these new settlers, and the work which will inevitably follow such as the building of branch railways, roads, schools, villages, and the many other capital expenditures which accompany the march of settlement.
I propose that the government inaugurate on a large scale a program which will bring about the settlement of the more or less scrub and lightly timbered land which we have in such abundance in our three prairie provinces -land with wonderful, almost inexhaustible soil, and easily reached by branch railways. In provinces like Manitoba, large areas easily drained might also be included. A most conservative estimate of this character of land easily available would be 10.000.000 acres capable of supporting 65,000 families, or roughly a quarter of a million farm population. This does not, of course, include Peace River. Here there is a minimum of 30,000,000 acres, even more fertile and more easily cleared that awaits development. The Peace River can and eventually will accommodate 175,000 families or nearly three-quarters of a million farm population greater than the entire population of the province of Alberta to-day. When considering these huge figures in connection with farm settlement we must add at least one-third more for the city, town, and village population which such development will necessitate and support.
I am sure that hon. members have in mind that we should first attempt to settle the 10,000,000 acres of vacant lands adjacent to our existing railways, and with this I agree.
I will deal with it later. For the moment, suffice to say that these lands when settled will add an additional 250,000 to our farming population and will mean much to the towns and villages on the existing railway lines where all modern conveniences now exist and where no new towns are necessary.
Summing up my proposal, hon. gentlemen will see that it contemplates the ultimate settlement of 50,000,000 acres of land by some
250,000	to 300.000 farmers. These, with their families, and the urban population which will be required, and the consequent developments which will follow will add 2 000,000 new people to the prairie provinces. I propose we start out to double the present population of the west. Do this and the rest of Canada will grow and prosper.
The title to the scrub lands I have referred to rests in the crown. This affords an opportunity to again advertise free homesteads. There is no inducement which compares with this: " One-hundred-and-sixty-acre farm free."
I suggest that these lands be given as homesteads to new settlers, free from all taxes for the first five years and subject only to ihe cost of clearing and the building of modest farm buildings.
I propose that only 80 acres, the easiest half of each homestead, be cleared leaving the balance to supply the needs of the farmer for building and for fuel. This he can clear himself later as opportunity offers. He will, however, to begin with, have 80 acres under plough, sufficient to support himself and family.
As to the cost of clearing, I have made careful enquiry into this question. It is no longer practical to clear land in the old fashioned way. The grub hoe must give way to the heavy steam breaking plough which walks through ordinary brush and scrub like so much
The Budget-Mr. McRae
