speechtext: Who pays it?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When Canadians manage
the world's greatest transportation system, the Canadian Pacific Railway; when we own and successfully operate the Canadian National Railways, with the largest mileage of any railway in the world; when we have in this country huge, successful, industrial enterprises in many lines of business, need any hon. member fear that we have no man in Canada big enough to give effect to the program for national development which I have outlined?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I ask the hon.
gentleman a question?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No; I have been listening
for two years to you fellows and I want you to listen to me for forty minutes.
I might point out to the government, however, that Providence cannot do this job for them. The success of such a large proposal is entirely a question of management, organization and administration. Worked out on a unit basis, this plan can soon be built up to locate 25,000 or 35,000 families a year.
It should be borne in mind, however, that once a good immigration movement gets under way it rolls up like a snowball. People will come along on their own and make their own arrangements. In a big movement probably not over 50 per cent of the immigrants would have to be provided for under the project I am suggesting. The others, attracted by the development and consequent prosperity, will locate themselves throughout the Dominion. If we handle 200,000 people a year under this government colonization program a total immigration may be anticipated of easily twice that number or equal to the maximum immigration the country ever enjoyed.
The settlement of the unoccupied lands adjacent to our railways is quite a different matter from the settlement of the crown lands with which I have been dealing. The title to the land adjacent to railway has passed
from the crown to private ownership. With a big colonization movement under way the best of these lands being near railways would be taken by incoming farmers with money. However, most of the acreage is the residue after years of settlement, and some other method must be adopted if they are to be colonized within a reasonable time.
The co-operation of the provinces is essential to settle these lands. It would be unwise to adopt any scheme by which the government would purchase them from the present owners. The practical method of colonizing them is under the crop payment plan, which gives the new settler a chance to pay for the farm out of the crop.
Two things are essential, first that the price be reasonable and that the settler have a few years to get considerable acreage under crop before being called upon to divide with the owner. Three years might be a reasonable time to grant him.
The provinces can do much to popularize the crop payment plan by passing legislation which will protect the owner of the land and relieve him from the necessity of sitting on the job when threshing time comes around. Absentee landowners cannot do this. A system of government supervision might be inaugurated in this connection.
In the second place as an inducement to encourage the owner to list his land for sale at a reasonable price, the province might well offer to waive the unoccupied land tax for those who listed their land for sale at an agreed price on the crop payment plan.
The province should work out some arrangement with the municipalities whereby these new settlers would be relieved of all taxes on their land for the first five years, thus putting them on a par with the homesteader. The prospect of being relieved from having to pay taxes on his land would also go a long way to make the scheme popular with the owners. This is a small price for the province to pay for a solution of its unoccupied land problem.
A well devised crop payment plan worked out in co-operation with the province is the only logical way of settling these lands by newcomers who have their wealth in brawn and muscle and not in cash.
New settlers need help and guidance when settling in their new home. The practical and inexpensive method, the one which proved so successful in the western United States a decade ago, is the organization of community clubs. The government should encourage these local associations by an allowance based on the number of new settlers located in their
The Budget-Mr. McRae

area. The compensation should be sufficient to enable the community club to maintain a paid secretary where the number of new settlers arriving justifies it. The community club can look after the needs of new settlers in their district very much better and cheaper than government inspectors. Experience has shown that these clubs develop into real colonization agencies. Enthused by the work, their members soon become active in soliciting immigration from their old homes. Something like this is necessary now that there are no longer large land companies at work keeping up interest in the community. The government might well make use of the enthusiastic residents of the towns and villages throughout the west along this line.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We do so now.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am surprised that the
hon. the Minister of Immigration and Colonization-a very successful farmer himself- has not seen fit to make use of the outstanding successful farmers throughout < the west as colonization agents, instead of the impractical brigade he now has on the pay roll. I say "impractical" for if my information is correct, many of his men have never lived on a farm, and others have never seen the district they are trying to settle. Compare their efforts with that of a successful practical farmer, sent back to his old home to solicit immigrants among his former neighbours, asking them to come and locate in his district. Many men in the towns and villages throughout the west are qualified to make equally competent colonization agents.
Picture these men as colonizers, with definite information of the available land in their community, the people, climate and conveniences, and what is even more important, a thorough understanding of the psychology of their old neighbours. Their word would be accepted, and well it might be. There would be no misrepresentation as frequently happens in colonization work. Hon. members will appreciate there is no comparison between the effectiveness of these practical men and the immigration agent from the city who either writes from his office or at most makes only an occasional trip into the country.
This is not a new idea. We employed it in the land business in western Canada years ago. It worked then. It will work now. The present chief land commissioner of the Canadian National Railways was this kind of a farmer colonizer when he was taken off the ranch twenty-five years ago.
It should be possible to send several hundred of these colonizers to Europe and the United States every fall. Most western men

have little to do in the winter. They would welcome an opportunity to visit their old homes. The cost would be small compared with the results-probably $1,500 each. Returning in the spring with their new settlers they would not only actually locate them on the land they had arranged for in advance but would continue a fatherly interest in them.
Here we have the real selection of immigrants. What chance has a ne'r-do-well to get over with this practically colonizer who knows his "no-good" friend would be sitting on his door step as soon as he got to Canada? This method of selecting immigrants is particularly applicable to those countries in Europe which do not welcome or permit our government to maintain an immigration office -countries we are now leaving largely to transportation companies. I have discussed this matter with Canadians, formerly Scandinavians, who assure me that they can go back to their old homes and bring out on an average twenty-five men, many of them with families, to settle on farms in the west.
It should not be difficult to get at least 300 of these colonizers at work every winter. Costing $1,500 apiece, it would require to finance them, less than half a million annually. These men should get at least 10,000 farmers a year including families, a total of probably 25,000 added to our population.
Hon. members should bear in mind that we now maintain all the staff that is necessary to instruct, supervise and direct these new colonization agents and to look after transportation for this increased immigration. Our principal trouble to-day is that we lack real practical men possessing the knowledge which is so necessary to get satisfactory results. Successful colonization is now an individual matter and must be conducted on that basis.
Referring to the question of provincial and federal co-operation in immigration matters, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, it is high time that our efforts in London were co-ordinated. Federal and provincial colonization officers acting on their own, competing with each other, do not make for the best results. Neither does it always place the new settler in that part of Canada Where he is most likely to succeed. Not a few of our immigrants fail because they have been misplaced in this far-flung Dominion.
It has always appeared to me that our High Commissioner in London should take a much more active part, and in fact should be the overseas head of our immigration and all other overseas work. Provincial immigration agencies, if necessary or advisable, should be

The Budget-Mr. McRae
housed in the same building as our federal immigration office. The High Commissioner should see that all our immigration work is harmonized and that Canadians are not unduly competing with each other.
One of the great problems in our immigration is practically disregarded. I refer to our unbalanced population-the excess of men over women-a situation which is rapidly growing worse. Immigration since the war has brought to us 170,000 more males than females. In the three prairie provinces in 1921 there was 185,000 more men than women. To-day it exceeds 200,000.
Anyone who travels through our prairie provinces; sees the desolate looking bachelor shacks by the hundreds from Winnipeg to the mountains, if he notes the adjacent more prosperous-looking homes of the farmer with a family, will realize what this unbalanced population is costing the country. On the farm one married settler is worth to the community as much as three or four bachelors- and I disclaim any intention to depreciate the honourable bachelors in this House. It is much more important to-day to bring a hundred thousand women to the prairie provinces than it is to bring in 100,000 men. Of course, it is more difficult. Nevertheless, a real effort must be made to get more women immigration.
So far no satisfactory scheme has been devised to meet this situation. A few domestic servants are brought in but not in numbers worth talking about. I suggest to the minister that he work out a real comprehensive plan and so far as humanly possible balance our immigration. He need have no fear of overdoing it.
The local colonizers I have suggested can bring back as many women as men and easily place them in their community. This, however, will only balance their effort and not help out on the 200,000 discrepancy which now exists.
I suggest to the Minister of Immigration and Colonization that he might with adequate1 financial assistance induce the Daughters of the Empire to take up this great work. They have chapters in almost every hamlet throughout Canada. What nobler effort could they be engaged in than transplanting throughout the Dominion, ten per cent of the two million surplus of their sex, now languishing in the British Isles. The necessity of this migration should particularly appeal to those who fear for the maintenance of British supremacy in the W'est. Give us British mothers and we need have no worry about the loyalty of our future generations.
Ever since the war we have discussed the problem of Imperial migration. So far little indeed has been accomplished. The London Morning Pest, a very conservative English paper states the case well. They say "Very little is done, and that the situation is a standing reproach and perpetual danger to the Dominion of Canada."
They express the willingness of Great Britain to take her share in schemes for Imperial migration but that the main responsibility for doing the greatest possible service to Canada, and to the empire, is upon us, and that matters cannot rest where they are without serious consequences. Quoting from the editorial, they say:-
An adequate scheme of settlement would involve considerable sums of money. But it is perfectly possible to solve these and other formidable difficulties when once the Dominions resolve to make it a part of their national policy to develop their resources with men of the British race.
Migration was doubtless the subject of much discussion at the last Imperial conference. Perhaps the Prime Minister will tell us why in this respect the conference has been so barren of results.
It should be possible to work out an adequate Imperial colonization scheme, when we have millions of acres of good land we want settled, and Great Britain has available both men and money.
I suggest to the government that no place in the British Empire affords a better opportunity for a big successful British migration than the Peace River country.
I want hon. members of this house, particularly from the east, to get an idea of the magnitude and the desirability of that great empire. In length it is about the distance from Windsor to Montreal with an average width of a hundred miles. In fertility and productiveness the soil is unequalled in any similar sized area in North America. The summer climate over a period of twenty years, is identical with Edmonton. The long summer days in the Peace River make it a safer crop country than much of the province of Saskatchewan already under cultivation. As for ;its winter, suffice to say that the hon. the Minister of Interior (Mr. Stewart) will, unless settlers interfere, soon be the largest rancher in the world. His buffalo, which roam the park-like country north, of Fort Vermilion, have increased to eight thousand and I am informed had a natural increase last year of twenty-five per cent. There need be no fear of the winters in a country where 'buffalo and their calves can thrive throughout tlhe year.
The Budget-Mr. McRae

1 fear, Mr Speaker, that many hon. members do not appreciate the proximity ol this country to the sea, which accounts for its climate. With good direct railway service, the heart of this district would be little over a calendar day's ride from the city of Vancouver. The Peace River country has been unfortunate in that two provinces undertook to provide it with transportation facilities. Neither of them completed their program and the country has been allowed to stagnate.
Railway facilities for this vast empire should be undertaken with a view to its ultimate development. Do not let us make the mistake we have made so often in the past, of building only with a view to the very near future. Peace River wants a trunk line to the sea-not a branch line outlet. We should broaden our vision. With a million people, the Peace River country will require not a single track to tide water but a double track railway to carry the product of its farms to market. Supported by proper development, the railway enterprises of both western provinces are worthy of completion.
I suggest to the government that in cooperation with the Imperial government and the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia the Peace River be developed as a great Imperial settlement.
Alberta and British Columbia together could furnish the land required for homesteads, thirty million acres The Dominion government could finance the cost of clearing the land and erecting the necessary buildings on the basis 1 already proposed. Great Britain as its part in the undertaking should finance the temporary requirements of the settlers, which it does now in part.
It would be a reasonable proposal for all partners in this British migration scheme to w'ork out. on some equitable basis, a joint guarantee of the interest for a period of twenty years of the bonds which our national railways would have to issue to enable them to take over and carry to completion the railway program of both Alberta and British Columbia including the branch lines which would be later required as settlement progressed. This would relieve the national railways from any danger of a deficit on account of this railway construction for a generation to come.
I share with my friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Clark) his great confidence in the British race, and his belief that they can and will make good fanners. I believe, however, that the preliminary training of these Britishers should be done at home so that the misfits would be largely eliminated there. To this end the British government

might see fit to transfer some of their dole funds as bonuses to induce farmers to train these prospective migrators.
Under an arrangement of this kind, almost a million men now on the farms in the British Isles could be made available for Canada. The lure of free homesteads, in a country British to the core, would attract them in large numbers.
It is not easy to establish a settlement of this magnitude, but this is the day of big undertakings. Many difficulties will arise, but the two great races who share this great Dominion have iD the past solved problems much more formidable. Peace River, with all its advantages, supplied with proper railway facilities, affords us our best opportunity for development. Have we the courage to undertake it? Where are our nation builders-the worthy successors of the Macdonalds, the Cartiers, and the Lauriers of yesterday?
An article appearing in the Financial Post as of March 2nd, indicates the probable immigration program of the government for the next few year3. Hon. members will see that the "Three thousand family scheme." is to be given a new dress and is to be known as the "Pioneer land settlement scheme." What hope would there be in this revamped plan with a government that has failed to complete the movement of only three thousand families in three years under the present scheme? How long is it going to take them at this rate to bring in 20.000 families as proposed? To appreciate the feebleness of this new effort it is only necessary to note that although the British wanted to send us five hundred families this year the Canadian government was unable to take care of them, and their movement is posponed until 1929. Let us be done with camouflage and makeshift. I appeal to the government to bring in an immigration program in keeping with the needs of the country.
The countries from which we will accept immigration have been dealt with very fully by hon. members during this debate. I want to say, however, that I believe it is the inherent right of every nation to decide its own racial status. I believe it is our bounden duty to posterity and to the fathers of confederation to see that, in the melting pot from which our future Canadians will be moulded, the blood of no race is allowed to enter which might undermine or weaken the blood passed down from our forefathers. Canadians must maintain the high standard they now enjoy. Ours is the right to choose; ours is the right to barr, and we should not hesitate.

The Budget-Mr. Senn
In his speech earlier in the session, the Prime Minister expressed a fear that if we prohibited Japanese immigration we might interfere with the development of our trade in the far east.
Mr. Speaker, I am supposed to be a business man. interested in trade, particularly in the orient, but I have not yet reached the stage- and I hope I never will-where I am prepared, in the interest of trade or commerce, no matter how important, to jeopardize the racial status of the Canadian people. I want to see all undesirable races absolutely barred, let the price be what it may.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house must have been very strongly impressed with the constructive speech which has just been delivered by my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. McRae). He speaks on the subject of immigration with some authority, because I understand that for a considerable length of time prior to the war he was actively engaged in the settlement of western lands, and in particular the settlement of the Saskatchewan valley. While thus employed the hon. gentleman conducted what was perhaps the most successful land movement that has ever occurred in the west. The Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Forke) having during his two years of office failed1 to evolve any progressive policy, I would com-mendl to his favourable consideration the suggestions which have been offered by my colleague, as coming from a gentleman who is eminently qualified to speak on this matter and to speak with authority.
It would be difficult at this stage of the debate to mention any phase of the tariff proposals which has not been discussed from some angle or other. Any contribution to this discussion, therefore, must necessarily be a repetition of arguments, and of facts and figures, which have already been advanced by my colleagues on this side of the house. The remarks which I have to make, consequently, will necessarily be very brief, and I can assure you, sir, that so far as I am concerned there will be no need to invoke the forty-minute rule.
Everyone I am sure must admire the clear and concise manner in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) always delivers his budget address. Unfortunately however, his budget proposals and his method of accounting are not so worthy of commendation. If I were to try to describe those proposals I would say that they were haphazard changes made in the tariff, without any consideration as to the results upon the industries affected, and not in pursuance of any governmental policy other 56103-74
than that of reconciling differences of opinion and quieting dissatisfaction in the Liberal ranks.
The record of succeeding budgets which have been brought down by this administration is one of constant and irritating changes in the tariff. The worst result of these changes which are constantly being made, is the lack of confidence which is evident in business circles throughout the country. Just the other day I was talking to a gentleman who is at the head of one of the large textile industries in Canada. After conversing with him for a while he told me he thought that by careful management and some changes in their methods of operation they would be able to carry on even under the handicap which has been placed on them by the present tariff changes; but there was a real note of anxiety in his voice as he told me two or three times during the conversation that he hoped these changes would be final. If there is one thing which is needed more than anything else in business circles and in industry throughout the country it is a feeling of security, but this cannot possibly be maintained unless we have permanence and stability in our tariff schedules. No business man can lay his plans for the future with any hope of sucess if he has no guarantee that his business is not likely to be disturbed and his plans thwarted by such tariff changes as have constantly taken place under this administration.
I should like to mention for a moment a fact which is so often referred to by hon. members on this side, that the Finance minister did not take into account the guarantees which have been given to the Canadian national railways when he was reckoning our national debt. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), if I am not mistaken, when speaking the other day, argued that because the government had never been called upon to pay any of the interest charges on these guarantees they should not be included in the debt. However the preliminary report of the Canadian National Railways which was tabled recently showed very clearly that the funded debt of the system had increased this year by something like $55,000,000, while the net revenues of the company were only sufficient to pay the interest charges on the bonds held by the public. On the other hand the interest on the million and a quarter dollars which has been advanced by the government in times past to the Canadian National Railways is still being added to the obligations of the system. So long as the road is not a paying proposition it is going to be very difficult for the Finance minister, or any other member

The Budget-Mr. Senn

of the government, to make the public believe that these guarantees should not be included in our national debt. They know well that if these obligations were included the debt would be very much greater than the Minister of Finance has indicated, and would be many millions more than it was when this government assumed office.
It has been very amusing to me, Mr. Speaker, to listen to ton. gentlemen opposite constantly repeating the statement that the country is prosperous. Listening to this constant repetition of the word " prosperity " one would be inclined to think that the Liberal members had become disciples of that famous man, Doctor Coue, who always told his patients that they should repeat over and over the old formula, " Every day in every way I am getting better and better ". Hon. gentlemen opposite may think they will lead the people to believe that Canada is prosperous, but I doubt it very much. Nevertheless by this constant repetition they may be able to induce some of their own number to believe the statement. Even a casual reading of speeches which have been delivered on the other side of the house would lead one to believe that those hon. members are not quite as confident in that respect as they would endeavour to lead the house and the country to believe.
I should like to mention very briefly one or two of the speeches which have been delivered. The hon. member who moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Ilsley) congratulated the government upon what he chose to call the abounding prosperity in the country, but before he had proceeded very far with his remarks he made it clear that, at least in the section of the country from which he came, prosperity was not nearly so much in evidence as some would have us believe. Again the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan) congratulated the government on the prosperous condition of Canada and in the next breath told the house that he represented a rural riding and that agriculture in that particular riding and district was not at all prosperous.
The hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) the other day made an excellent address in the house, but I am afraid she somewhat lessened the effect of that address by her statement that members of the Conservative opposition were a party of snobs or words to that effect. I have been in this house for some years and I am sure that the hon. member who spoke in that way has always been treated by members on this side with every courtesy, with all the courtesy which has been due to her as an hon. member.

Indeed it is possible she has received a greater amount of deference than the average member on account of the fact that she is the only lady member of the house. I think therefore that her remark was not very well advised, and if she had time to think it over she would never have made it. During the course of her remarks she mentioned the fact that the hon. member for South Huron had stated that the rural districts are not in a prosperous condition and she agreed with him. I find myself this afternoon, for once at least, in agreement with those two hon. members. I cannot however agree with the remedy proposed by the hon. member for South Huron for the unsatisfactory condition of agriculture in Canada. His remedy, as I understood it, was to have freer trade relations. The constituency which I have the honour to represent lies in close proximity to one of the largest manufacturing centres in this Dominion and much of the produce of the farms in that community is taken to that city and consumed there. In the constituency which I represent we have four large creameries and one of them of which I have been a patron for quite a number of years disburses annually to its patrons, the farmers of that locality, something like a million dollars in cream cheques. The bulk of the produce of that creamery is taken to that city and other cities in the vicinity where it is sold and consumed. Not only the produce of those factories but other produce of the farms is taken to those cities where it is consumed-butter, milk, cream, eggs, poultry, apples and other fruits of all kinds, potatoes and other vegetables; and considerable quantities of the meat products which are produced on the farm are taken to that city and others for consumption.
The value of the home market cannot be over-estimated. It is the greatest asset which the farmers, particularly of the province from which I come, possess to-day. Lower duties such as were suggested by the hon. member for South Huron would inevitably mean injury to industry and consequent unemployment and a lower wage Beale. That lower wage scale in the end would' mean considerably less in the way of buying power on the part of the people who purchase our commodities. There is no doubt that at-the present time marketing is one of the most serious problems which confront the Canadian farmer. That is proven very clearly by the fact that co-operative organizations are springing up all over the country for marketing home products, and perhaps the best example which we have of that in Canada to-day is the western wheat pool. I for one

The Budget-Mr. Senn
am glad indeed that the western wheat pool has proved a success, but the very success of that enterprise forms perhaps a real danger to it and to other enterprises of a similar nature. It has been the history of co-operation throughout Canada that up to a certain point in their operations organizations of this kind have always been successful; but after they have attained some measure of success their directors possibly think they have reached the point where they can branch out and undertake other lines of operations which very often lead to disaster. We have in Ontario a form of co-operation which has been successful for many years. I refer to our farmers' mutual fire insurance companies. I believe the reason for their success has been chiefly that they have been under strict government supervision and inspection and that their powers have been clearly defined by law. I would suggest to my hon,. friends from the west, who are interested in the wheat pool and other similar organizations, and to the government as well, that the time must come in the near future when the operations and powers of these organizations must be defined by statute and their books must be subject to government supervision and inspection. That would add very much to the security which they would have and people who are interested in those organizations would, as a result, have greater confidence in them.
I want just for a moment to mention something that has been so often repeated in this house that it may seem like foolishness to refer to it. In connection with the problem of marketing agricultural products we have had a real case where marketing has been interfered with by freer trade relations. I refer to the Australian treaty and the preferences which have been extended to New Zealand whereby butter is coming into this country at a nominal duty of one cent per pound, where originally the duty was considerably higher. The duty on butter coming into Canada to-day is lower than similar duties in any of the other British dominions. For years prior to the ratification of this treaty the surplus of butter exports from Canada was constantly increasing; but in the three short years which have passed by since this treaty came into effect the surplus of exports has been on the decline until to-day we find there is a surplus of imports, and the change in the past three years has been approximately 35,000.000 pounds of butter. These figures have been enlarged upon at considerable length by hon. members who have already spoken and therefore I do not intend to go any further into the matter.
56103-74i
The great danger to the industry in my judgment is not that butter is coming into Canada from these other sister dominions but that the price of butter in this country to-day is controlled by cables which are coming from those particular countries. It really makes very little difference to us whether butter is coming into the country or not so long as our farmers have to sell their butter at prices which are being quoted to Canadian dealers by cables from Australia and New Zealand. It is a common axiom of the dairy industry that producers should receive at least ten cents a pound more in the winter months than in the summer months for their butter. It is known of course that production costs are much higher in the winter than in the summer, and it is manifestly unfair to ask our farmers to compete with farmers in New Zealand and Australia who are producing butter under summer conditions the year round. So far as this treaty is concerned, I am afraid that the farmers of Canada will not agree with the member for South Huron in his contention that we should have freer trade relations to benefit agriculture.
But, Mr. Speaker, the tariff schedules as brought down in the budget proposals in regard to the woollen industry are calculated to injure another branch of agriculture, namely, the sheep industry. The placing of yarns on the free list will mean a consequent loss to the wool growers of the Dominion. It is only during the past few years that the wool growers of Canada have been able to realize a reasonable price for wool, and this is only because the sheep industry has declined to such an extent that Canadian wool is at a premium. It is estimated that the people of Canada use about eighty million pounds of wool annually. This is calculated on a grease basis, or as the wool comes from the back of the sheep. Of this, about half is used by the woollen and knitting mills of Canada, and the remainder is imported in the form of yam, manufactured goods, or goods that are further advanced than yarn. This means that there is a demand at the present time in Canada for approximately forty million pounds of wool, of which there is produced in Canada less than eighteen million pounds. Unfortunately, as a result of the changes proposed in the budget, many more pounds of yarn are likely to be imported, which will mean a consequent diminishing of the needs of our woollen mills in the matter of raw wool, so that the present proposal to admit certain yams free of duty will be a real detriment to the sheep industry of Canada. This is particularly unfortunate in face of the fact that the Ontario government is taking special steps and spending
The Budget-Mr. Senn

money to build up the sheep industry in Ontario and induce farmers to keep more and better sheep.
Anyone who is conversant with the woollen industry will admit that the mills in Canada are just as up to date and as well equipped as those of any other country in the world. Last year while the house was in session the woollen manufacturers' association placed an exhibit of goods produced in Canada in the Chateau Laurier. Many bon. members took advantage of the opportunity to examine these goods, and I am sure that everyone was firmly convinced that the products of our Canadian mills stand second to none in the matter of quality. Yet we find that because of the cheap production costs and low price of labour in the British Isles and in France, there are lines in which our woollen mills are unable to compete with Great Britain and France because of our higher standards of living and the higher wage scale. Our wage scale is dependent very largely upon the price of labour in the country to the south of us. From time to time many of our best woollen operators have been induced to go to the United States because the mills in that country are able and willing to pay the price.
During the past year the woollen manufacturers' association made certain representations to the tariff board. In his annual address the president of the woollen manufacturers' association stated that briefs had been presented to the tariff board, showing that of woollen and worsted cloth there is a market in Canada for about 5540,000,000 worth each year, and that only one third of this market is now being supplied by Canadian mills, the remaining two-thirds of the market being supplied by workers in mills in other countries. Another brief showed that of white blankets of a total of $906,000, the Canadian production was approximately $275,000 as compared with $631,000 imported-33 per cent produced in our own Canadian mills, and 67 per cent imported. Socks and stockings of wool show a total consumption in Canada of $5,396,000, the production in Canada amounting to approximately $2,800,000, while the imports amounted to approximately $2,600,000-55 per cent produced in our own Canadian mills, and 45 per cent imported. Of yam, of a total Canadian consumption of $6,400,000, the production in Canada amounted to $2,860,000, while the imports amounted to $3,545,000-45 per cent produced in our own Canadian mills and 55 per cent imported. In regard to knitted outerwear, while it was impossible to arrive at the exact figures owing to the way in which import and production statistics were prepared, it was clear that the

importations of certain classes of knitted outerwear were very heavy indeed.
There is no reason to suppose that our mills could not produce practically all of these goods which are required to meet the needs of the Canadian people, and this in turn would not only give employment to many hundreds more of our people in mills which are now either entirely or partly idle, but would also be a boon to the sheep industry.
The British manufacturer is pretty well satisfied with the tariff changes which have been proposed in regard to the woollen industry. I have before me a periodical published by the woollen industry of Great Britain, called the Weekly Wool Chart and Private Business Report, of the week of February 23, 1928, published in Bradford, England. It contains on editorial on the tariff reductions which have been brought down by the Minister of Finance which I should like to quote. It says:
A revision of tariffs is embodied in the new Canadian budget. Greater protection has been obtained for the Canadian manufacturing industry, not by increasing the duties on fully-manufactured goods, but by reducing the duties on yarns and grey goods. Imports of yarns for weaving from the United Kingdom (formerly charged 10 per cent) will be admitted free. Dress goods, and so forth, in the grey will be admitted at 10 per cent (against 15 per cent), which automatically increases the preference from 7J to 124 per cent. Dyed goods continue to pay as before, except that dyed cloths weighing under 5 ounces per square yard (lustres, linings, and so forth), are to pay 5 per cent less than the present rate (24J per cent), the reduction also applying to France. It will be remembered that last year the Canadian manufacturers applied for increased protection, and Mr. J. H. C. Hodgson and Mr. George H. Wood went out from Bradford to give evidence before the tariff board against the application. The educational work which they did has evidently been of good service.
That is how the British manufacturer views the changes that are being made in our tariff. The British manufacturer knows as well we do that these changes mean an increased preference for British goods in the markets of Canada, with a consequent diminishing of the sale of our own goods.
There are several changes made in the present budget which will work out very harmfully to the woollen industry, one or two of which I would like to mention. The placing of yarns for weaving, on the free list will without doubt have the effect of very seriously injuring the spinning industry in Canada. Many mills which are to-day spinning their own yarns will have to purchase the cheaper yarns coming from the British Isles if they are to compete in our markets with foreign made goods. But there is another

The Budget-Mr. Bancroft
danger which is perhaps not quite so apparent and which the minister cannot have taken into consideration. It is that there are certain mills in the country which are both weaving and knitting. These yams are supposedly admitted free of duty to be used for weaving alone and great care should be exercised to see that they are not used in the knitting business in competition with other mills which are spinning their own yams for knitting purposes. Might I suggest to the minister that if he insists upon having worsted yams for knitting coming into the country free of duty, his intention should be carried out by means of a 99 per cent drawback when it has been clearly demonstrated that these yarns have been used for weaving purposes alone.
Another tariff item which will work a great deal of harm to certain industries in the country is the placing of a duty of 15 per cent on mercerized cotton yarns coming from the Uinted States, where formerly these yarns came in free. This will be of no advantage to either the Canadian or the British manufacturer of mercerized cotton yarns. Under this item imports must still be made from the United States because even with the additional 15 per cent duty, these yarns can be imported from the United States more cheaply than they could from the British Isles.
As an example, may I furnish a quotation on what is known as double forties of C. P. mercerized cotton yarns landed from England, duty free and quoted at 89A cents per pound, while the same goods from the United States, after paying the 15 per cent duty, are quoted at 76 cents per pound. I am told that the larger concerns using this material will be compelled to pay anywhere from ten to twenty thousand .dollars a year extra for their material, and that there will be no benefit derived by any Canadian industry.
These are some instances in which the woollen trade will be adversely affected in Canada and there are others which I hope to bring to the minister's attention when the tariff resolutions are before the committee. The placing of machinery for these factories on the free list is viewed as a farce by the companies, many of which have a large amount of machinery already standing idle.
Taking into account these few features of the present budget which I have endeavoured to present to the house, I am fu'lly in accord with the amendment to the budget as moved by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan). I cannot believe that the budget will improve the unemployment situation in Canada or relieve the position
in which agriculture finds itself, and I therefore intend to support the amendment and to vote against the budget.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take part in this debate until I heard on Monday last the speech of the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Boys). In that excellent speech he dealt with the binder twine industry, but from one angle only, and because of that I feel called upon to present what might be termed the other side of the case.
He asserted that the removal of the duty on binder twine in 1898 had ruined this industry. He intimated that more binder twine had been imported each year than had been consumed in Canada. He said that, of nineteen companies manufacturing binder twine in 1908, only two are manufacturing binder twine at the present time and that the Brantford Cordage Company was being forced out of business because of imports of binder twine from Holland and Germany. It might be well at this stage to look into the history of the binder twine business in Canada. Previous to 1895 binder twine carried a tariff of 12J per cent, in 1895 this was reduced to 10 per cent; in the budget of 1897 the tariff was wiped out entirely, becoming effective January 1, 1898. In 1893 a wealthy American from New York city came to Canada and decided that the protection, 12J per cent, was sufficient to warrant the formation of a twine and cordage combine. There were eight twine factories in operation in Canada at that time. They were merged into one corporation and six of them were closed. This all happened under 12J per cent protection.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And the Tories were in
power.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. The combine immediately increased the price of twine about 50 per cent. Shortly 'after this the federal government purchased some of the idle machinery from one of the closed factories and began making binder twine in Kingston penitentiary. About the same time the Patrons of Industry formed the Farmers' Binder Twine Company at Brantford. From 1894 to 1900 this company never paid less than 10 per cent dividend annually and in 1901, three years after the tariff had been wiped out, they paid the enormous dividend of 250 per cent. They were able to pay this abnormal dividend on account of conditions resulting from the Spanish-American war and its effect upon the stock of raw materials on hand. This large dividend paid to farmers in all parts of Ontario gave rise to the opinion that large profits could be made from the
The Budget-Mr. Bancroft

manufacture of binder twine. Two promoters from Montreal capitalized this temporary condition in the binder twine industry by promoting companies and selling stock for the erection of binder twine factories at Walker-ton, Ontario, Chatham, Ontario, and Brandon, Manitoba. Before this idea of making easy money from the manufacture of binder twine had subsided, companies were formed and mills erected at Ayton, Peterboro and Brantford. Many of these new mills were conducted by men who new little or nothing of the business, and most of them were shortlived.
As I do not intend to take the full forty minutes allotted to me, and as I iam discussing only one subject, I should be very pleased, Mr. Speaker, if you would call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
April 1st to September 30, 1927, being the first six months of the fiscal year 1927-28 the imports from Holland rose to 11,964 300 pounds. But, Mr. Speaker, during those three years the imports from the United States had decreased. The imports from the United States for 1925-26 amounted to 39,184,480 pounds, while for 1926-27 the imports from United States dropped to 18,061,000 pounds, and for 1927-28 they fell still further to 6,910,200 pounds. So that during the past three years the total imports into Canada have decreased considerably each year. The Brantford Cordage Company Limited has had a splendid record. It began in a small way in 1901, and to use its own words, " has steadily increased and expanded its business and extended its factory from time to time until 1925 ". Since then it has claimed to be in difficulties. These difficulties are of their own making. They are trying to pay dividends on too much watered stock, and the Canadian farmer is not willing to pay for such folly.
The hon. member stated that free trade had not reduced the price of binder twine, but that as a matter of fact the price was raised and is now much higher, and he has put upon Hansard a table showing the price of binder twine beginning with the year 1913, He shows binder twine to have cost 9 cents a pound in 1913 and 14 cents in 1926. Now the whole level of prices has risen in the same period.
The index number of wholesale prices in Canada, as compiled by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, shows that prices rose generally during the whole period he covered. If we take prices in 1913 as 100, prices in 1926 are represented by the number 156, or, in other words, the purchasing power of money declined between 1913 and 1926 in the ratio of 100 to 156. Binder twine costing 14 cents a pound to-day would be of the same actual value as binder twine costing 9 cents a pound in 1913; so that the rise in price shown in the hon. gentleman's table means nothing so far as free trade in or protection of binder twine is concerned. The price of binder twine bore the same relationship to general wholesale prices in 1926 as it did in 1913, and in 1927 the price was 12 cents or two cents lower than 1926. In other words, binder twine was actually cheaper in 1927 than in 1913, having regard to the variation in the purchasing power of money in these years.
That leaves out of account the great improvement in the quality of Canadian binder twine since 1913. Any hon. member who has used a grain binder over that period will bear me out in this. This improvement in quality has been brought about through the use of a better quality of fibre, and the use of improved machinery in the factories. A study of the trade figures and the reports issued by twine manufacturers shows that this industry has expanded and prospered under free trade. Its growth compares quite favourably with other industries operating under protection over the same period of years. No mergers have been formed. The quality of the product has improved and the farmers are being supplied with a high quality twine at a reasonable price. The companies engaged in this industry have had periods of expansion and periods of depression, similar to those experienced in other industries. Naturally the binder twine industry is directly affected by the acreage sown and the character of the season. Disinterested study of conditions affecting the binder twine industry must lead to the conclusion that it has benefited from the removal of the duty as much as any single industry, operating in a country where protection is the general rule, can benefit. Its experience supports the contentions of the advocates of a low tariff and there can be no question that the results have been of considerable advantage to the grain growers of the Dominion, so much so that the imposition of a protective duty on imports of binder twine would arouse very great resentment among the farmers of Canada.

In regard to telegraphs, there are three telegraph systems in Canada, the Canadian National, the Canadian Pacific, and the Western Union. The Canadian National, starting at Vancouver, where it has cable connections, runs across the country and ends at Moncton. The Canadian Pacific, starting at Vancouver, where it has connections, runs across the country to Nova Scotia, where it has cable connections. One' difference between the two lines is that the Canadian Pacific terminates on the eastern seaboard, while the Canadian National terminates at Moncton. There is a gap of 198 miles between Moncton and Halifax, where some of the cables are. That gap is not completed by the Canadian National, but the Western Union comes in there and continues from Moncton to Halifax, picking up the communications. The Western Union is the sole telegraph system in Prince Edward Island; it algo is the sole system in a portion of New Brunswick and in a portion of Nova Scotia. The Western Union is an American line; it is not Canadian. If one wishes to send a cablegram from Ottawa to London and goes to the Canadian National office, the message will be sent by the Canadian National to Moncton, where it is transferred to a foreign company, the Western Union, and transmitted over an American cable. If the message is sent by the Canadian Pacific, it proceeds from Ottawa and later passes over a considerable mileage through the state of Maine, and finally reaches Halifax, where it connects with the cable. In the ordinary course, messages sent from Ottawa going Canadian Pacific are transmitted over an American cable, and messages sent by the Canadian National are transmitted over the Western Union, and go over an American cable. If the sender thinks about it and wishes it done, both companies will send the message over British cables if the sender so specifies, but it is only on request that the cable messages are sent in that way.
Three years ago, when I had the opportunity of speaking to the house, an arrangement with the Canadian National could not be effected; that is, at that time the Canadian National could not transmit a message across the Atlantic by the imperial cable because they had no connection, and they had to use the Western Union. To that extent there has been a 
change since that day. Messages from London to Ottawa are sent over the imperial cable, a government-owned cable, and are then transmitted over the Canadian Pacific, although it passes through a large section of the state of Maine.

Mr. Speaker, as this debate has continued several weeks it is becoming very difficult to develop any subject which has not already been pretty thoroughly discussed. I have noticed that hon. members from all quarters of the house have expressed a wish for peace, happiness and prosperity for the people of Canada, but the methods they suggest for securing that happy condition of affairs vary very much. The hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) a few days ago pointed out that hon. members opposite of the Conserva-
The Budget-Mr. Gershaw

tive party and of the Progressive group had expressed entirely divergent views as to how the varying interests of Canada could be harmonized, and it seems to me that the government occupies a central position, being pushed in one direction by our Conservative friends and in the other direction by our Progressive friends.
We have in this house representatives of the two great historic parties and as well the representatives of the Progressive and Labour groups. The Liberal party has a traditional fiscal policy, as I understand it-to maintain the lowest tariff possible. True, the' government is not working in that direction as fast as some of us would like, but that, I submit, is the fiscal policy of the Liberal party. And I believe that the great majority of the people are in favour of such a tariff policy. For instance', the representatives of the Progressive and Labour groups, who have been sent here by those producers and workers who did not feel that they were being properly represented by either of the old parties,

those representatives favour a low tariff. Then we have the Conservative party, who retain their traditional fiscal policy of protection. I take that for granted after reading an editorial which appeared in the Montreal Gazette on Monday, definitely stating that the policy of the Conservative party is one of protection. True, it is noticeable by the tone of the resolutions that passed at the Winnipeg convention and by the remarks of some members of the official opposition that they are to some extent departing from the policy of Sir John A. Macdonald, a policy which he contended was admirably fitted to fully develop the Dominion of Canada as it was in his day.
Now, I am convinced that a great number of our people believe that the tariff should be- kept as low as possible, for very good reasons, one of these being that, as is pretty generally conceded, the price of any article or commodity increases as the tariff thereon is raised; and the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bancroft) showed conclusively this afternoon that as the tariff is reduced on any article or commodity its price decreases accordingly. It seems to me that competition from within too often is not sufficient to maintain prices at their proper level, and that we need outside competition to attain this end. Then again, Canada has great natural resources, and if our industries are to be prosperous they must be based on those natural resources. It is scarcely fair for any industry to ask that it be protected to the extent of 35 ot 40 per cent, for this enhances prices and the people under present conditions should not be forced to buy the products of that industry. 
I had intended to discuss the question of immigration, but it was so thoroughly dealt with this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. McRae)-and no one is better qualified than he to speak on the question-that I do not deem it necessary to do so. I was glad to hear the applause which greeted his statement that in any policy of land settlement our own young men should be given as good an opportunity to participate in its benefits as any immigrant.
WTe have been told that the national revenues are buoyant, that Canada is in a good position financially, and that there is very general prosperity throughout the country; and the reason I made bold to rise to-night was to suggest some1 ways in which those revenues might be used to great advantage. We desire to encourage the tourist business in every possible way, because it is very profitable for the Dominion, and in the near future large expenditures will be required on highways. We shall also require to continue branch railway construction. In many of our outlying districts the people have to go many miles to a market, and there is very great need for railway facilities, especially in the western part of this country. Further branch lines have been definitely promised, and the people of those districts have tried again and again to secure their fulfilment, but they are still living in hope that something will be done at no distant date. I believe much money will need to be spent in this direction. During the war and the years immediately following the war very few public buildings were constructed, and I noticed when the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) was trying to get his estimates through, several members pleaded for poat offices and other public buildings in their constituencies. It seems to me that in the near future a great deal of money will have to be spent for this purpose. Then again technical education will have to be supported by grants from the federal treasury. The government in the past has done a good deal in this direction, and I am sure that many of us will be sorry that the grants are not being continued. Another source of expenditure which confronts us is in aid of the various provincial governments. Many of them to-day are having great difficulty in balancing their budgets. The government of the province of Alberta has had to report a deficit in spite of pretty careful management.
An hon. member remarked the other day that Canada suffered a great deal from the war, and that around our tables there are at least fifty thousand vacant chairs. But besides those who made the supreme sacrifce we

The Budget-Mr. MaeNutt
see on our streets many returned men who still bear the sears of war service, and we know that many of them are suffering now from diseases attributable to their service overseas. The stress, the strain and the anxiety of those days is now beginning to affect the health of many of those who were fairly sound at the	conclusion of hostilities.
It is quite -clear that more money will have to be spent for pensions. I have been told by a reliable authority that during the month of February just passed eleven hundred new claims for pensions were filed, 96 per cent being from men who had never before taken that step. Canada went wholeheartedly into the war, and took her full share of responsibility. No one regrets that, and surely no one is unwilling to do his or her share in recompensing those for the personal sacrifices which they made overseas.
No one will challenge the assertion that those best able to pay should bear a greater share of taxation, and at the present time I do not think any of us would object to paying the present rate of income taxation. In view of the great need of money to meet the expenditures to which I have drawn attention I think taxation should be reduced very gradually. It seems to me that as taxation can be reduced the customs tariff should first receive attention, then the sales tax, and last and least of all the income tax. It is hardly fair for us to compare our income tax with that of the United States. There the government obtain about 65 per cent of their revenue from income tax, while we obtain only 14 per cent. Besides, Canada was in the war from the very beginning until the armistice.
Now, as to the subamendment proposed by hon. members directly opposite, it contains much that appeals to me. The fact that the income tax has been reduced certainly is a matter for regret. The fact that the sales tax has not been eliminated is not quite so clearly a matter for regret, for I believe it would be a hardship to remove this tax all at once. It would deprive the treasury of a great deal of revenue, and it would be unfair to many retail merchants who have goods on their shelves on which they have paid the sales tax, and they would have to sell these in competition with goods purchased after the removal of the sales tax. It is true some reduction has been made in the customs tariff but, as I said before, I should like to see a greater reduction in that direction. There is much that appeals to me in the subamendment, yet I should not like to vote for it if it meant turning the government out of office.

Mr. Speaker, before proceeding to discuss the subject now before the house I desire on behalf of the bon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Smith) to read a letter which he had not finished on Wednesday last when his time expired. This letter is from the Oxford Manufacturing Company of the town of Oxford in the county of Cumberland, and is as follows:
We were stunned to read the portion of the Robb budget dealing with the textile industry. We were suspicious that the Tariff Advisory Board was but a gesture, and it has so worked out. The agricultural interests of this country were entitled to have counsel before this board, but there is no good cause why the * Bradford Chamber of Commerce, representing the woollen manufacturers of England, should have anything to say as to the regulation of tariff matters of this country. From 1878 to 1897 this industry was developed to great proportions, but the demise since then has been gradual under the bane of constantly decreasing protection. The application of the manufacturers before the Tariff Advisory Board was very complete, and in addition to this a brief was presented to Hon. Mr. Robb by the Canadian Woollen and Knit Goods Manufacturers' Association, reference No. 42, touching on the tariff and conditions in this and other countries for more than one-half a century back. It should be only necessary to show that in this country we make only 30 per cent of the woollens used, but evidently the discrimination against this industry must go on. It is impossible to believe that the Tariff Advisory Board, if unfettered, could otherwise than recommend some measure of help for the manufacturers of woollen cloths. Instead of protecting the employees of this industry against foreign labour, Mr. Robb has wiped away the duty on weaving yarns, which means, but for the small number of workers employed in the weaving and finishing of the cloth, this commodity can be brought in now absolutely free. We doubt very much if the minister of the department realized this. In any case, the blow has been struck, and the end is not far away for the average woollen manufacturer. Not in twenty years have the changes in the tariff endangered the life of the woollen industry as this one.
You will note that in the case of 40's and finer yarns a small duty has been added. This is no help, of course, as only the worsted mills spin this fine. In the medium size yarns which are commonly made here the duty has been cut. We need to have our case placed before the government through a royal commission. The manufacturers should combine together and elect one man to fix prices, wages and other conditions and to see that these are adhered to.
Yours very truly,
The Oxford Manufacturing Company, Limited.

I can quite understand, Mr. Speaker, why the hon. member for Cumberland was anxious to place this letter before the house and the country, representing as he does a constituency which has been struck harder than perhaps any other portion of the province of Nova Scotia. I am sure that as a representative of that county he does not wish to see any more smokeless chimneys left standing as monuments to the tariff tinkering of t;he present government.
In looking at the budget in general, as it affects the whole country, I think we should congratulate ourselves that as it has been presented it is not very revolutionary. The general public attitude seems to be that it will neither kill nor cure anybody or anything. Being a canny Scot, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has developed the habit of playing safe, but on this occasion, with so many widely divergent views to meet, his task has not been one of [DOT] sun clear simplicity. He had to prepare a budget the chief Object of which was to glorify the King government, and for this purpose there had to be more shadow than light in his financial statement. The arts of concealment and manipulation, the drawbacks and shifts made to get around awkward facts, make this tissue of tricks a very shallow performance. With a Barnum like belief in the general gullibility of mankind, the minister has endeavoured to ride two horses and serve two masters, and of course he will come to the inevitable fall. Someone said long ago that you can fool all the people some of the time and some of the people all the time, but you cannot fool all the people all the time, and I think that is a very true saying at this time in our history.
We regret to observe that the minister is beginning to show signs of the strain of his office, in endeavouring to reconcile the many conflicting elements which surround him. Some of these hon. members want a low tariff, some want a high tariff and some want no tariff at all. On this side of the house we are very fond of the Finance minister; we like his geniality, and1 we very much regret to learn that he is desirous of relinquishing his portfolio. May I make the prediction that if the minister can retain his portfolio for one or two years longer the people of this country will probably give him a much needed holiday.
I read a letter concerning the textile industry in Nova Scotia, and I think the changes in the textile schedules are the most extensive and drastic contained in the present budget. The whittling and nibbling at the steel and coal schedules have been so ably dealt with by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) and many other hon. members that at this time I will not attempt to make any ex-
tended reference to them, except to remind the Prime Minister once again that we in the maritime provinces accepted his pledge in good faith when he stated that the assistance recommended by ,the Duncan commission would be given, or at least dealt with, during the present session. It is a very disappointing situation which we face to-night. A few weeks ago the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) journeyed down to the city of St. John and made an announcement which is reported as follows in the press:
The government had implemented all the recommendations of the Duncan report except two, the Valley railway project and the bounty to Sydney steel plant. The two matters were, however, receiving the serious consideration of the government, and with in a few weeks the policy would be divulged, which he thought would make every maritimer feel proud.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) speaking last year in the city of Sydney and elsewhere, boasted that the government had fulfilled the recommendations of the Duncan commission one hundred per cent. The utterances of these two ministers remind me of the practice which exists at present in our northern country where for a good many months of the year transportation has to be carried on with dog teams. The owners of those teams in that northern country, I am told, always have one or two loose dogs.which are trained to go out unharnessed in advance and bark in order that their barking and their activity should encourage the team doing the hauling. The barking of the two ministers referred to were given, doubtless, for the purpose of encouraging the government to do what they were pledged to carry out but which pledges I am sorry to say have not been fulfilled.
I feel disappointed that the Minister of National Defence, speaking from his place in this house a few days ago, should have stated that the government would give serious consideration to granting the assistance to the steel industry of Nova Scotia which the Duncan commission had recommended whenever the following conditions would be met:
First, there must be unity between the coal and steel companies.
Second, there must be a shrinkage of the capital so that the industry will have an opportunity of earning dividends on some reasonable investment.
Third, the unwieldly organization should be simplified. It now consists of some fourteen companies.
Fourth, there ought to be co-operation between the provincial and municipal authorities in the work of building up this great industry. With the litigation ended and these conditions met, the way will be open for serious con-

The Budget-Mr. MacNutt
sideration by the federal government of the presentation of the real and legitimate needs of the industry.
That, Mr. Speaker, was the most disappointing announcement I have heard since coming to this house three sessions ago. A year ago among the maritime members there was a diversity of opinion regarding the action we should take at that time, and some of us dissociated ourselves from the ideas that others had expressed in that respect. To-night, after the recent statement of the Minister of National Defence, 1 must say that the majority of us who urged giving the government more time, in other words, to hold out the olive branch and afford the government further opportunity to deal with this question, were wrong, and those who opposed that course were right. Let me say that down in the province of Nova Scotia we all admire the Minister of National Defence as a brilliant lawyer, we admire him as a gallant soldier, but after his recent announcement we cannot admire him as a statesman or a politician. I believe that had the Minister of National Defence and the Postmaster General said to the government in regard to these great basic industries-which in my judgment means more to the people of Nova Scotia than all the other industries dealt with in the recommendations of the Duncan commission-that they would pack their trunks and go home, we would have had before us to-night legislation which would have given that industry the same fighting chance as other steel industries in Canada enjoy. I believe that the assistance which the Duncan commission recommended should be given that industry as it is the only assistance that would place it on a footing with other steel industries in Canada.

And whereas the Duncan commission on maritime claims recognized the coal and steel industries as important national assets and recommended certain measures necessary to help establish these industries;
Therefore resolved that the parliament of Canada should adopt a national fuel steel policy which recognizes Canada's need of coal and steel and Canada's ability to fill that need, the aim of which policy being to produce in Canada the coal and steel consumed in Canada so far as that is at present possible and to take the necessary steps to secure expansion of these industries so that there may be ultimate and complete fulfilment of this national policy;
And further resolved that the recommendations of the Duncan commission on behalf of these industries should be immediately implemented.
That is all I wish to say at the present time regarding the existing situation as to the nonfulfilment of the recommendations of the Duncan commission in reference to steel. May I also refer briefly to another matter to which previous speakers have made very little reference? The Duncan commission advises the apointment of a minister or a deputy minister of fisheries, but I have heard no reference whatever by the government in regard to this appointment. It cangot be that the government lack men on that side of the house who are practical fishermen. Possibly the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) has more knowledge of the fish business than any other hon. gentleman sitting on that side of the house. I remember a few short years ago that the hon. member for AntigonishjGuysborough accompanied the Premier on a speaking tour throughout Canada to the Pacific coast, and I am sure that if at that time the hon. member was of such calibre that he could occupy a position on the platforms of this country with the Prime Minister, he should be capable of filling the position of deputy minister or minister of fisheries. The people
The Budget-Mr. MacNutt

of the maritime provinces are looking forward to the appointment of someone to fill this position, They believe that will solve many of their difficulties and, as before stated, I cannot think that it is for any lack of suitable members from the maritime provinces on that side of the house that the position has not been filled. May I suggest that before many weeks pass the position which I have indicated, that of a deputy minister or a minister of fisheries, should be filled?
I should like for a moment to refer to that portion of the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), which transcends all other questions in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, as a matter of fact, in the whole province of Nova Scotia. I refer to the government having made no provision in the budget for the preservation of our domestic markets for Canadian farm and dairy products, nor any reference to legislation for the effective development of the natural resources of this country. Let me first point out that dairy farming in Nova Scotia, and particularly in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, is carried on most extensively, and notwithstanding the fact that hundreds of petitions and resolutions from all Canada have been forwarded to the government praying that the duty be increased on importations of butter from Australia and New Zealand, the government thus far have turned a deaf ear. The hon. member for Queens (Mr. Sinclair)-and I regret he is not in his seat to-night-who followed me a few weeks ago in the debate on the address, contended that prices of daily butter had not been decreased by the importations of butter from Australia and New Zealand. In this view the hon. member for Queens is entirely at variance with the dairymen in his province and, indeed, throughout Canada. I have before me a most interesting address delivered a few %ays ago by Mr. J. A. Macdonald, of Charlottetown, dairy superintendent for Prince Edward Island. I think it was the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Macdonald) who referred to this matter in his speech a few *weeks ago. The address is such an admirable one that I should like to see it printed and sent out to the people of this country. Mr. Macdonald, who is in the employ of the Liberal government of Prince Edward Island, closed that interesting address in the following words:
At the present time our markets have received quite a set-back, owing to so much New Zealand butter being dumped into Canada. Up to November first, 100,000 boxes of New 
Zealand butter was exported to Canada, and one boat in November delivered 34,000 boxes in Halifax.
New Zealand and Australia are producing, under summer conditions, and are bonused to the extent of six cents a pound. So you see why we cannot compete with that trade, and make a profit with our type of cow.
That is a statement by the dairy superintendent of Prince Edward Island.
