speechtext:
I should like to have placed on Hansard some statistics which were given in answer to some questions by the hon. member for South Oxford' (Mr. Cayley) dealing with importations of butter; but I find that Hansard has already been loaded up with a great deal of the same statistics and I will let that feature pass for the present.
A few weeks ago in this house I stated that in the constituency which I represent 1,400 of our best milch cows had been shipped away, mostly to the United States. I had some doubt whether my figures were correct, so I

The Budget-Mr. Peck
wired to one of the leading dairymen in my county, and the day after I made that speech I received the following reply:
Over three thousand shipped out of province Colchester alone shipped two thousand.
(Signed) C. P. Blanchard.
That was some weeks ago. Mr. Blanchard, I may say, is one of our leading Nova Scotia dairymen, a good friend of mine, and a good friend of the Liberal government. I also have a letter here from him informing me that the Borden Milk Company in the town of Truro have announced that if the farmers continue to dispose of their herds, the company, being unable to secure the quantity of milk that they require in their factory, will be forced out of business. The Borden Milk Factory, I may add, is the oldest condensing plant on the American continent- not in Canada alone, but on the continent of America-and I say that if such an old-established plant is driven out of the country because the fanners of the district are unable to make a profit from their herds, due to the importation of New Zealand butter, it will be another tragic addition to the already large number of silent factories and smokeless chimneys.
The hon. member for Queens (Mr. Sinclair), speaking in the debate, said that the reason the Americans were buying cows in Nova Scotia was because they could buy them cheaper. I confess they can buy them cheaper, but why is that so? It is simply because the farmers are going out of the dairy business, and their cows are being sent to the United States, where the farmers are protected to the extent of 12 cents a pound on their butter, 20 cents on a wine gallon of cream, and 2i cents on a wine gallon of milk; and there is a bill before congress to-day proposing to increase the duty from 12 to 16 cents a pound on butter, and on cream not over 45 per cent butter fat from 20 cents, which is the present duty to 30 cents a wine gallon, and from 2} cents, the present duty, to 7i cents per wine gallon on milk. That is why our ccws are going to the United States.
I promised an hon. gentleman who interjected a remark a while ago to give him certain figures, which I will now do. At the ninth annual meeting of the national dairy council of Canada, held in Toronto on November 21, 1922, the council voted to ask the government to terminate the Australian treaty. Only three days ago a delegation of the National Dairymen's Association of Canada, which has a membership of 250,000 and is representative of all the dairying interests
in this country, waited on the government at Ottawa, and I had the pleasure of meeting the president of that association and discussing this question with him. Incorporated in the memorandum which they presented were resolutions from every dairymen's association from Nova Scotia to British Columbia, all referring to the great injury that was being done the dairying industry of Canada by the large amount of Australian and New Zealand butter which has entered Canada since September last. It was shown that at the port of Vancouver, 386,340 pounds of Australian and 6,738.000 pounds of New Zealand butter, and at Halifax 5,704,440 pounds of New Zealand butter, had arrived in this country, making a total importation of nearly
13.000.	000 pounds. In addition to that, it is expected that a boat load will arrive at either port every two weeks until the end of March, w'hich means that Canada will receive more than 15,000,000 pounds of Australian and New Zealand butter in this session alone. It was also shown that this had the effect of lowering the price of butter fat to producers from 3 to 5 cents a pound.
The memorandum also estimated that the
15.000.	000 pounds of imported butter, had it been produced in Canada, at 200 pounds per cow per year, would require 75,000 cows, averaging 10 cows per farm, and would require 7,500 farms giving employment to as many farmers and their families. Canada has the lowest tariff on butter and cheese of any dominion in the British Empire, it being one cent per pound as against 12 cents per pound in Australia.
I desired to speak on the question of the natural resources of this country, but time will not permit, and I shall therefore discuss it at a later date.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I venture to tender to you my congratulations upon the change made in the rules of debate, chiefly, I believe, upon your recommendation. There has been some criticism of the new rules, but I believe they have been of considerable advantage. They have had two results: One is the elimination of the long and tedious speeches to which we were accustomed to listen, and the other is the advantage, if it is an advantage, of introducing into the debate the newer and younger members.
I wish to address a few remarks to the hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Forke), who I am sorry is not in his seat at the moment, but perhaps I may venture to address him through Hansard. I want to appeal to him, as other hon. members

The Budget-Mr. Peck

have done, to reverse his decision with regard to the MeConachie child. As the matter now stands, unless the minister changes his decision, the result will be that husband and wife are separated, and the children do not get the advantage of the mother's help and comfort at an age when they so much need her care. The only reason why these people are compelled to be separated is because of the fact that the youngest child, a mere infant, is said to be weak-minded. If this is so, is there any harm in allowing that child to enter Canada when we get the advantage of receiving immigrants whom we need to the extent of a man, his wife, and four other children? There are weak-minded people in this country at the present time, and we are not suffering a great deal; and it will not hurt very much if another weak-minded person is allowed to come in. The minister's reason for his decision, as stated in the house, is that he is tied by regulation, but the Immigration Act is the only legislation controlling the situation, and section 4, which has already been quoted in the house, reads:
The minister may issue a written permit authorizing any person to enter Canada or, having entered or landed in Canada, to remain therein without being subject to the provisions of this act.
The act is clear; surely there is nothing in it to prevent the minister from issuing that permit if he sees fit.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That question
came up a day or two ago and it was suggested that it be referred to the Department of Justioe for a ruling. I am informed that the department has given its ruling, maintaining that section 18 is the controlling provision; and under that section the minister is not permitted to exercise discretion.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should be very glad to see that decision. At any rate, the act seems to me to be clear enough. One would think that any lawyer or layman would infer, when an act says something, that it means what it says. It is suggested, however, that the matter is also affected by a regulation, but the regulation could scarcely be of greater force than the act itself. But even if there is a regulation that can very readily be overcome, because it must be confirmed by order in council and an order in council could be obtained changing the regulation to meet this particular case. This case is one that has excited a good deal of interest, and as the matter now stands it is a reflection upon the Dominion if these people are to remain separated. Some effort should be made to

reverse the decision, and I submit that the minister should make it possible for these people to be brought together again.
I want to refer now to the question of population, and also unemployment-two matters which are closely related. There is no doubt that the country stands in need of population; everyone agrees with that. It has been stated by many leading citizens that what is needed for the development of the Dominion is an addition to population. The railway officials are strongly of that view; Sir Henry Thornton has referred to the matter several times in public addresses. Here we have two railways, efficiently managed, excellently equipped, running on time and giving good service, the officials all endeavouring to do what they can to promote the interests of their respective companies. Yet we find the Canadian National actually unable to meet its financial engagements for lack, as Sir Henry Thornton has said, of a larger population to provide increased freight and passenger traffic, which would enable him to put the railway on a better footing. Along the same line we hear from the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
Not only is our population stationary, but in the past few years a great many people have moved to the United States. That is a fact which is uncontradicted; indeed it is borne out by the government statistics. The matter is therefore one deserving the careful consideration of the government. Why should so many people in this rich country find it necessary to move to another land to make a living? It is said that we are unpatriotic in pointing out these facts. It seems to me that we should be unpatriotic if we did not point them out, the facts being as they are, with a view to obtaining, if possible, some solution for the problem Which is presented to us.
The people of Canada are very favourably treated in having had assigned to them such a substantial portion of the earth's surface for management and development. Canada is a oountry of which we are all proud, a country embracing the northern half of the American continent, bounded by the Atlantic and the Pacific. Yet with all its wealth and untold resources, its large timber limits, its arable lands and its minerals, we seen to be at a standstill and cannot attract the population we have a right to expect. Those who have left Canada for the United States have done so for what they considered good reasons; and the foremost reason was that they were unable to find employment at home. The crying need of this country is

The Budget-Mr. Peck
an opportunity for people seeking employment to obtain suitable work whereby to earn enough to maintain themselves and their families. The labour problem is a most important one for the country to cope with. And in so many respects this government has failed to give to the labourers, to those seeking employment, the protection they should have.
Let me point out how in three substantial respects this government has failed to deal with the question of labour, and failed thereby to maintain in the country the population which we should have. In the first place, Canada fails to manufacture for its own people, to the extent that it should, the natural supplies which are needed. Secondly, we allow the removal from the country, in raw or only slightly manufactured form, of the natural resources of the Dominion. And we fail to encourage the manufacture of our raw material for our own use. Let me illustrate what I mean when I say that we fail to manufacture in this country, for its own use, the natural supplies which the country needs. We imported for consumption last year over $500,000,000 of manufactured goods, a large portion of which should have been manufactured in Canada. We have been discussing the woollen industry at some length, and the claim made by those engaged in that industry for protection. Apparently the protection which existed before the proposed change in the tariff was not sufficient to conserve the woollen industry to the manufacturers of Canada, for we imported last year in woollen goods, not including raw wool, products to the value of $43,000,000. Of iron and its products out imports totalled $248,000,000. That includes automobiles and parts, $65,000,000; machinery $46,000,000; farm implements $26,000,000; engines and boilers $16,000,000. We also imported electrical apparatus to the extent of $18,000,000. All these goods, or at any rate a very large proportion of them, could have been manufactured in Canada, and as a matter of fact they would be manufactured here if the government would only give to the industries engaged in their production reasonably sufficient protection. These goods to which I have referred amount in all to $300,000,000. If only half of that amount had been manufactured in this country, estimating at 50 per cent the wages which would enter into their production, there would have been expended in Canada in employment and wages $75,000,000.
Even the farmers of Canada are not protected as they should be. One would have
56103-75J
thought that this country was the last word in agricultural production; yet we find that under all the trade treaties, which apparently will not prove satisfactory, we imported last year, of the three items, eggs, meat and butter, $9,500,000 worth. Tobacco has been discussed in this debate; and of tobacco, unmanufactured, we imported $7,000,000. Of fresh fruits we imported $24,000,000. Of course many fruits included in these exports we do not grow in Canada; I have been unable, therefore, to make the necessary classification. At any rate, the imports of fruits of the varieties produced here form a substantial part of this amount, and certainly we could produce them in Canada.
Now I come to the question of exports. We export far too much of our raw material, material which should be worked up and manufactured in this country. Here again Canada has lost considerably by its failure to provide opportunities for labour in the manufacture of these goods. I notice that our exports of grain products amounted to $447,000,000; while metals amounted to $154,000,000; wood, unmanufactured, $101,000,000; and paper, $129,000,000, making a total export in these four classes of $831,000,000. The paper represents resources which are certainly not inexhaustible, and unmanufactured wood is in the same category. This exportation of wood and paper means a drain on our natural resources, which we shall not be able to replace within a limited time. The metals of course have gone, but we have so many opportunities of investigating the possibilities of our hidden metals in Canada that possibly we shall not feel this very seriously. Of grain, our main export was wheat, $339,000,000, and wheat flour, $60,000,000, making a total of $399,000,000. Only 8 per cent represents the manufactured article; the rest is exported in the raw condition to other countries where the work of preparing it for use provides employment for foreign labour.
Under the third head, there are industries which should be developed in this country. If this were done a large amount of employment would be provided for labour here. The coal industry is one that should be dealt with; in fact, it must be dealt with. It has been much discussed but apparently no solution for the question of moving coal from the eastern and western sections of the country to Ontario and Quebec has yet been proposed. It is, however, only a question of time before this will have to be done. It seems most unfortunate, however, that in the meantime we should be purchasing in another country the coal which we need to maintain our industries and supply our homes. We

The Budget-Mr. Peck
imported last year from the United States $53,000,000 worth of coal, which under proper management could have been taken from our own mines and applied to our own industry.
I shall discuss only one of the many changes which are proposed in the tariff resolutions before the house, and I refer to this matter only because it affects an industry in my own city. I have reference to the weaving of yam. We had some assurance last year from the government, represented at the time by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), that no attempt would be made to interfere with existing industry. The statement which was presented to the house had been carefully prepared and it was read by the Minister of Railways representing, as I say, the government. I presume it was intended to appease the Liberal-Progressive element in the house. This is what the Minister of Railways said:
We shall move forward cautiously with the aid of knowledge of the facts secured by the tariff advisory board toward the goal of making our tariff structure bear as lightly as possible on production, industry and the people generally-
That is something of which probably all of us could approve; it is a vague, general statement. But this is more specific:

having always in view the greater prosperity of all the legitimate industries of Canada.
With the present proposed tariff changes before us, can it be said that these changes are made with a view to the greater prosperity of all the legitimate industries of Canada?	_	,
There has been a good deal of discussion during this debate in connection with the woollen industry, and the proposed reductions have met with a very general opposition. I refer particularly to the weaving yarns, because that is an industry which exists in my own town, employing some 180 people. There are other workers engaged in that line in my city, but they are employed in the carpet and rug business, which I understand is not affected by this tariff. What does this mean? Certainly it means that this industry in Canada will have to face increased competition, which will be a hardship on the manufacturer but will result in a greater hardship on those engaged in the shops carrying on that business. The working man is the one affected most by these tariff reductions which interfere with that industry. To the manufacturer it means a reduction in salary, a reduction in dividends and perhaps even the passing of a dividend, which is a very serious matter to him. To the worker, however, it means a reduction of wages or a lay-off from work, because he is the 
primary sufferer from anything which interferes with the production of the article in the manufacture of which he is engaged, and it is the workmen for whom I feel the greatest regret. I know many of them in Peterborough and I know how they have been affected already by the conditions obtaining in the woollen industry. They have not been working full time as it is, and this is simply going to add an additional hardship to those under which they have been labouring for some time past. I trust that the matter will receive further consideration before these tariff changes are adopted by the house; I believe something should be done to help those people to whom I refer.
I can only say in conclusion, Mr. bpeaker, that I intend to support the amendment proposed 'by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan).
